A Texas transfer on death deed (TOD deed) lets an owner name a beneficiary who receives the real estate at the owner's death, without probate for that property. The law is Estates Code Chapter 114, and a deed only works if it is recorded with the county clerk before the owner dies. This guide covers what the statute requires, what the beneficiary receives and how to sell the house afterward.

How a TODD works in Texas

A transfer on death deed (TODD) lets a Texas owner name who gets a piece of real estate at death, with no probate case for that property. It comes from the Texas Real Property Transfer on Death Act, Chapter 114 of the Estates Code, which took effect September 1, 2015.

The deed does nothing for the beneficiary during the owner's lifetime. The owner keeps the house, can live in it, mortgage it or sell it, and the named person has no ownership claim yet. For a seller, that detail matters more than any other: a TODD is no obstacle to a sale made during the owner's life.

What the deed must contain

It must look like an ordinary recordable deed, say the transfer happens at the owner's death, and be recorded before that death. Section 114.055 sets those three requirements, and the recording goes in the real property records at the office of the clerk for that county.

  • Only an individual can make one, and the owner needs the same mental capacity required to sign a contract.
  • A power of attorney cannot be used to create it.
  • Nobody needs to tell the beneficiary, and no payment or acceptance is required.
  • No warranty of title comes with the transfer, whatever the wording says.

A deed that is signed but never recorded before death does not work. Ask the clerk in that property's county how to file it, and use a Texas attorney if the title has liens, multiple owners or a divorce in its history.

Canceling or changing a TODD

A TODD is revocable under Section 114.052, no matter what the deed itself says, and the owner can revoke it until death.

There are two ways to do it, and both have to be recorded before the owner dies in the same county records as the original:

  • A later TODD that replaces the earlier one, either by saying so or by conflicting with it.
  • A written revocation, acknowledged after the deed it cancels.

A will cannot revoke or override a recorded TODD. This catches families by surprise: the will may leave the house to one child while a recorded deed names another, and the deed controls. A divorce judgment revokes the deed as to a former spouse named as beneficiary, but only if notice of that judgment is recorded before the owner's death.

Can I still sell my house after signing a TODD?

Yes, an owner may sell, mortgage or give away the property at any time. Section 114.101 says the deed does not limit the owner's right to transfer or encumber the real estate, and the buyer's rights are unaffected even if the buyer knows about the deed.

A later sale cancels the TODD for that property once the new deed, or a memorandum giving notice of the sale, is recorded in the same county before the owner dies (Section 114.102). The practical steps for a seller are simple: sign the sale deed, record it, and let the title company handle the rest. Under that same section, a TODD in the chain of title does not trigger a due-on-sale clause or create new disclosure duties during the owner's life.

The deed also leaves tax benefits alone. Homestead rights and property tax exemptions for homeowners, people 65 or older, and people with disabilities stay with the owner while alive.

What happens to the house at the owner's death

The beneficiary gets the property if that person outlives the owner by 120 hours. If there are several beneficiaries, they take equal undivided shares with no survivorship right between them, unless the deed provides otherwise.

The beneficiary takes the house subject to whatever liens, mortgages and other interests existed at death (Section 114.104). A beneficiary who inherits a mortgaged home still faces the lender, and a lender may treat the claim in a probate case as a matured secured claim or a preferred debt and lien claim if a personal representative is appointed. A beneficiary also has the right to disclaim the property under Chapter 122.

The property is outside the probate estate, but not beyond reach of the owner's debts. If the estate cannot pay claims, administration costs, estate tax or certain family allowances, the personal representative can pursue the transferred real estate, and suits must start by the second anniversary of the death (Section 114.106).

Selling an inherited TODD house

The usual path is to record proof of death and then sell like any other owner. A TODD transfer needs an affidavit of death and a death certificate recorded with the clerk for the home's county.

Before listing, work through this checklist:

  • Get certified copies of the death certificate.
  • Pull the recorded TODD and confirm it names you and carries the right recording stamp.
  • Record the affidavit of death and death certificate in that county's deed records.
  • Ask the lender, the tax office and any homeowners association for payoff and balance figures.
  • Check whether the owner's estate has a pending case that could pursue the property for debts.

Any title company reviewing the sale will expect a tidy chain. If another heir contests the deed or the estate owes debts, closing can stall, so sort that out before accepting a contract.

TODD, Lady Bird deed and will compared

All three can pass a house at death, but they differ in how much control the owner keeps and what happens to the title.

Ways to pass a Texas house at death
ToolProbate for this houseOwner can still sellCan a will override it
Transfer on death deedAvoidedYesNo
Lady Bird (enhanced life estate) deedAsk an attorneyYes, without the beneficiary's consentAsk an attorney
WillNeeded, or a muniment of titleYesIs the controlling document

No official form exists for a Lady Bird deed, which is a reason to have a lawyer draft one.

Mistakes that cause TODD trouble

Trouble usually starts with timing and records. The usual causes include never recording the deed, recording it in the wrong county, and forgetting that a will cannot cancel it.

  • Recording after death. The deed is ineffective if it is filed late.
  • Joint owners. A deed signed by one co-owner revokes only that owner's part, and a deed made by joint owners with survivorship is revoked only if every living joint owner revokes.
  • Divorce or remarriage with no update to the records.
  • Assuming the home is shielded from debts, which Section 114.106 does not allow.

When the home is a rental, a fixer or an unwanted inheritance, a cash sale to a home buyer can be a way to skip repairs and listing work. Whichever route you pick, confirm the recording is complete first.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Texas transfer on death deed avoid probate?

Yes for that property. The real estate passes to the beneficiary at death outside the probate estate, but creditors and the personal representative may still reach it if the estate cannot pay valid claims, within two years of death under Section 114.106.

Where is a TODD recorded in Texas?

Record it with the clerk of the county containing the land, and do it while the owner is alive. Check that clerk's rules and fees before you file.

Can a beneficiary refuse a TODD property?

Yes. A designated beneficiary may disclaim all or part of the interest under Chapter 122 of the Estates Code, as Section 114.105 provides. Speak with an attorney before disclaiming because it affects who receives the share.

Does the beneficiary get a warranty of title?

No. A TODD passes the real estate without any covenant of warranty, even if the deed contains wording that suggests otherwise, so a buyer or heir should rely on a title search and title insurance.

Can I sell the house after recording a TODD?

Yes. The owner can sell or mortgage at will, and the buyer's rights are not affected even if the buyer knows about the deed. Recording the sale deed in the same county before death makes the earlier TODD void as to that buyer.

Lady Bird Deed in Texas: What the Law Says and What to Do

If you hold or inherited a house conveyed by an enhanced life estate or lady bird deed, we can look at it as-is. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas statutes do not use the term "lady bird deed." We searched the full text of Property Code Chapter 5 and Estates Code Chapter 114 and found neither "lady bird" nor "enhanced life estate.

Holding an enhanced life estate deed?
Tell us about the property. We can review it as-is and explain how a sale would close.
Get My Cash Offer →

What a lady bird deed is

A lady bird deed is the popular name for an enhanced life estate deed. It names who inherits a house while the owner keeps full ownership and control for life. The owner can live there, sell the property, and change or revoke the deed at any time. The instrument comes from common law, so no Texas statute spells out its form.

There is also no official form. Sample language shows up in legal publications, and a lawyer should review any version before you sign, because a drafting mistake can have serious consequences. Since the deed names the person who takes the house at death, it can move real property outside probate, the same goal a will pursues through the court.

A seller who holds a house this way faces different questions than an owner with a plain warranty deed. Who has to sign, what the lender thinks and what the county clerk needs on file all depend on the wording of the recorded deed.

Lady bird deed, transfer on death deed and life estate compared

The gaps matter most when a sale is on the table. A statutory transfer on death deed (TODD) falls under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code, the Texas Real Property Transfer on Death Act. A lady bird deed does not.

Lady bird deed and TODD side by side
FeatureLady bird deedTransfer on death deed
Legal basisCommon lawEstates Code Chapter 114
Backup beneficiariesNot allowedAllowed
Mortgage due-on-sale clauseMay sometimes be triggered at the owner's deathNot triggered (Sec. 114.101(5))
Signed under a power of attorneyPossible if the power of attorney authorizes itNot possible (Sec. 114.054)
Warranty of titleGeneral, special or noneNone allowed (Sec. 114.103(d))
Selling and creditor claimsMay be hard to sell without the beneficiary's approvalProperty stays open to estate creditor claims for two years after death (Sec. 114.106)

An ordinary life estate deed is a different animal. The beneficiary gets an interest right away, so the owner generally cannot sell or mortgage without that person's consent, sale proceeds are shared, and the beneficiary's creditors or a divorce court can reach the interest. Those deeds are mostly permanent, while the enhanced version can generally be changed or revoked.

Can I sell a house held under a lady bird deed?

Yes, because the owner keeps full control. The comparison above does warn that a sale can be hard to complete without the beneficiary's approval, so a buyer's closing agent will read the recorded deed first. Have a certified copy ready and expect questions about whether the beneficiary needs to sign.

  • Lender issues. A mortgage may carry a due-on-sale clause that a lady bird deed can trigger at death, so ask the servicer about the loan before relying on the deed.
  • Signature authority. If an agent under a power of attorney signed the deed, the power of attorney itself must have authorized that kind of transfer.
  • Warranty language. A deed can carry a general warranty, a special warranty or none, and the closing agent will see which applies.
  • Recording. The deed has to be signed and acknowledged to be recorded, and it is filed with the county clerk of the county where the property sits (Property Code 12.001(b)).

If you change your mind about who inherits, an enhanced life estate deed can generally be revoked. Do it with a recorded document prepared by a lawyer, not informal notes.

Medicaid estate recovery

A lady bird deed is sometimes used to shield real property from Medicaid estate recovery claims. It may work in some cases, and whether it works in yours is a question for an elder law attorney.

Texas Health and Human Services runs the Medicaid Estate Recovery Program (MERP). It reaches only long-term care services received after age 55, and only for people who began receiving them after March 1, 2005. Nursing facility care and several waiver programs are covered, such as STAR+PLUS long-term care services and Community Attendant Services. The state never asks for more than it paid, and it weighs debts such as funeral costs and a mortgage before a claim is paid.

  • No claim is made while a spouse is alive, or when there is a child under 21 or a child who is blind or permanently disabled.
  • No claim is made when the estate is worth $15,000 or less or the Medicaid costs are $5,000 or less.
  • An unmarried adult child who lived in the home full time for at least a year before the death can also stop a claim.
  • Heirs may ask for an undue hardship waiver and must provide proof.

For a specific case, the agency's contractor can be reached at 800-641-9356. The agency also looks back up to 60 months at asset transfers made before an application for nursing home or waiver services, so the timing of a deed can matter.

After the owner dies

The beneficiary named in the deed takes the house without a probate case, but the county records still have to show it. Practice form books include an affidavit of death used to transfer title under a transfer on death or lady bird deed, and a TODD needs an affidavit of death and a death certificate recorded with the clerk where the property sits. Ask the clerk or a title company which documents they expect for the deed in your file.

When no such deed exists, other paths apply. A will can be probated within four years of death. A muniment of title lets a will prove ownership when the only debts are real estate liens. A small estate affidavit works for estates of $75,000 or less, not counting homestead and exempt property. Texas repealed its inheritance tax effective September 1, 2015.

On the property tax side, a beneficiary who moves into the inherited house applies for a homestead exemption with the appraisal district. An heir not named on a recorded deed gives the district an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate and a recent utility bill. School districts must grant $140,000 off the value of a residence homestead, and owners age 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000.

Where to get help

Start with a lawyer who handles estate planning, since law libraries will not tell anyone what the law means for their own situation. The Legal Help page on the State Law Library's site lists ways to find one. Law libraries also keep practice forms, among them a lady bird deed form in Texas Estate Planning and another in Davis's Texas Estate Planning Forms.

Two more references are worth handing to the attorney who drafts or reviews your deed: Texas Administrative Code Title 1, Section 358.350 on life estates and remainder interests, and Property Code 5.009 on the duties of a life tenant.

If you inherited a house through one of these deeds and want to sell it, send us the recorded deed and the basic facts. We buy houses as-is, and the closing agent will confirm which documents the county clerk needs before the sale.

Frequently asked questions

Is a lady bird deed legal in Texas?

It is an enhanced life estate deed that rests on common law. No statute defines it, so the wording of the recorded deed controls what it does.

Can I sell my house after signing a lady bird deed?

Yes. The owner can live on the property, sell it, and change or revoke the deed. Expect the buyer's closing agent to read the recorded deed and ask about any mortgage.

Does a lady bird deed avoid probate in Texas?

It can move the house to the named beneficiary outside probate. The beneficiary should still record the paperwork the county clerk requires.

Is there an official Texas form for a lady bird deed?

No. Sample language appears in legal publications, so have a lawyer draft or check the deed.

What is the difference between a lady bird deed and a TODD?

A TODD is created under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code and allows backup beneficiaries. A lady bird deed rests on common law and cannot name alternates, and it may trigger a mortgage due-on-sale clause.

Texas Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: Rules and Removal

Squatters or a Title Dispute on Your Texas Property? Get a Cash Offer

Dealing with an unauthorized occupant or an inherited house with unclear possession? We buy houses as-is. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has two different things people call squatters rights: adverse possession, a claim to ownership that takes years, and a 2025 sheriff removal process for people who unlawfully entered a home. Adverse possession is in Civil Practice and Remedies Code Chapter 16. The removal process is Property Code Chapter 24B, effective September 1, 2025. This guide explains both from the statutes.

Dealing with an occupant you cannot remove?
We buy houses as-is, including ones with occupants or title questions. Tell us what is going on.
Get My Cash Offer →

Do squatters have rights in Texas?

No Texas law rewards a person for just moving into someone else's property. Still, a long, open and hostile occupation can eventually become ownership through adverse possession. Separately, a newer removal process lets owners clear certain trespassers without a full lawsuit.

These are two different tracks. Adverse possession is about who holds title after years of occupation, and it is decided in a trespass to try title case. Removal of an intruder is about getting someone out of a property now. A homeowner preparing to sell needs to know which situation applies, because a person living in the house can complicate a closing.

If you are unsure which track fits, start by writing down when the occupant arrived, whether you ever gave permission, and what happened when you asked them to leave.

How Texas defines adverse possession

The Civil Practice and Remedies Code defines it as an actual and visible appropriation of real property, begun and continued under a claim of right that is inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another person (Section 16.021(1)).

Every term in that wording matters. Anyone walking by, including the owner, should be able to see the possession. It must rest on a claim of right, and it must be hostile to the owner, meaning the possessor does not hold with the owner's permission. A renter who pays the landlord is there by permission, so that occupancy never turns hostile to the landlord's title.

A claim is brought through a trespass to try title suit, in which a judge decides who holds the better title.

Time periods

The best known period is ten years under Section 16.026, and title passes if the possessor stays for the whole period and meets the statutory requirements. Shorter periods exist where the possessor has paper title.

Adverse possession periods under the Civil Practice and Remedies Code
SectionPeriodMain condition
16.0243 yearsPeaceable adverse possession under title or color of title
16.0255 yearsPossessor cultivates, uses or enjoys the land, pays taxes and claims under a duly registered deed
16.02610 yearsContinuous possession meeting the statutory requirements

Confirm the current statute text with an attorney before relying on the shorter periods.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How an owner can remove squatters

Under Chapter 24B of the Property Code, an owner may hand the sheriff or constable a removal request and skip the courtroom, as long as every listed condition holds.

  • The occupant stayed after being told to leave.
  • The property was not open to the public when the occupant entered.
  • No lawsuit is pending between the owner and the occupant.
  • The occupant is not a family member or a current or former tenant.

Section 24B.005 lets someone wrongly removed sue the owner, so the request has to be accurate. When the person is a tenant or former tenant, the removal process does not fit, and the owner turns to the eviction route instead.

The eviction route

Eviction starts with written notice to vacate, usually three days or more, or whatever longer period the lease sets, and then a suit in justice court.

Service on the tenant has to happen at least four days ahead of trial, and the court sets the hearing between 10 and 21 days after the suit is filed. Either side may appeal to county court within five days of judgment. After a final judgment, a writ of possession becomes available six days later, and an officer must give 24 hours' notice before removal.

A summary disposition procedure, Section 24.0051606, exists for squatters in a forcible entry and detainer suit. The response is due in four days, and a disputed case goes to trial between 10 and 21 days after filing.

How a squatter or adverse possessor affects selling

A person living there without a lease can hold up a sale, since buyers and lenders expect to receive the property empty, and a title company may refuse to insure over an open ownership claim. Resolve the occupancy first, or tell the buyer exactly what is going on.

Hold on to proof that you own and control the place: your deed, recent tax bills and copies of any written notices you served. Paid tax records help show who has been treated as the owner. If you are the person who has occupied a property for years, speak to a lawyer before you claim anything, because a mistake can cost the whole claim.

  • Do not change locks or cut utilities on a tenant without legal advice.
  • Photograph the property and keep dated copies of every notice.
  • Ask the sheriff or constable's office how to submit a removal request.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property taxes and adverse possession

Tax payment is part of the five-year rule in Section 16.025, which asks that the possessor pay taxes and hold under a duly registered deed. For owners, a clean tax record is useful evidence that you have acted as the owner.

The owner at the start of the year decides who owes that year's tax, and in most cases a bill still unpaid on February 1 is delinquent. An owner who lets the bill lapse while someone else occupies the house invites a second problem on top of the first.

Risks of a wrongful removal

Using the sheriff or constable process against a person who is really a tenant or family member exposes the owner to a lawsuit under Section 24B.005. That is why the four conditions in the statute matter.

Before you file, ask yourself whether the occupant ever paid rent or had permission to stay, whether any suit between the two of you is pending, and whether the property was open to the public when the person entered. If the answers are unclear, a justice court eviction case gives both sides a hearing and a written judgment, which is a safer base for a sale contract.

The notice you must send before suing is set out in Chapter 24 of the Property Code, and a 30-day federal notice may apply to covered properties. Check your property's status before you serve a three-day notice.

A seller who has been through any of this should tell the title company at the start, since a past dispute can show up in the records they search.

Steps before you list

Work out who is living in the house before any buyer tours it. Put together a short timeline of the occupancy, gather the deed and tax receipts, and decide whether the occupant is a tenant, a former tenant, a relative or a stranger. That one answer tells you whether you are on the eviction track, the removal track, or in a title dispute.

Once the house is vacant, you can list it normally. A buyer who pays cash can close faster than one who needs a lender, but the title company will still want any court judgment or removal paperwork in the file.

Frequently asked questions

How many years of adverse possession does Texas require?

Ten years is the best known period under Section 16.026. Shorter periods of 3 and 5 years apply in narrower situations that involve title or a registered deed.

Can a tenant claim adverse possession of a rental?

A tenant who pays rent holds with the owner's permission, so the possession is not hostile to the owner. Hostility is part of the statutory definition.

Can I remove a squatter without going to court?

Sometimes. Chapter 24B allows a removal request to the sheriff or constable when the occupant is not a family member or current or former tenant and no suit is pending between you.

How long does a Texas eviction take?

Hearing dates fall 10 to 21 days after filing, and a writ of possession is available six days after final judgment. Appeals and other issues can add time.

Can squatters stop me from selling my house?

They can delay it, since buyers and title companies want a clear title and vacant possession. Sort out the occupancy with an attorney before you list.

A Texas eviction starts with a written notice to vacate, then a sworn petition in the justice court of the precinct where the property sits, and it ends with a writ of possession executed by an officer. The rules are in Property Code Chapter 24 and the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure. This guide walks through the statutory steps landlords follow and what each deadline is.

The Texas eviction process in four stages

Four stages make up a Texas eviction: written notice to vacate, a justice court suit, a judgment, and a writ of possession served by an officer. A landlord cannot skip ahead and remove a tenant personally, and every stage has its own timer.

Rule 510 of the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure sets the procedure for the justice court case. This page follows the court side. Rules for the notice that comes first are on the eviction notice page.

Step one: the notice to vacate

A landlord starts by serving a written notice to vacate. The usual period is three days, or the period in the lease (Property Code section 24.005). Acceptable delivery: in person to the tenant or a household member aged 16 or older, posted inside the premises in an obvious place, by mail, or by e-mail if the written lease permits.

A tenant who paid on time the month before gets a pay-or-vacate demand. Federal CARES Act properties may need 30 days. Because Rule 510 does not reach pre-suit notices, chapter 24 of the Property Code is where landlords look.

How the justice court case runs

Suit begins with a filing in justice court. The tenant must receive papers four or more days before trial, and the court sets the hearing between day 10 and day 21 after filing.

Unless summary disposition is in play, the tenant need not file a written answer. A jury request is due at least three days before trial. Under Rule 510 a rent claim up to $20,000 can be joined to the eviction. Amendments to that cap have been proposed, so the court clerk is the person to ask about the current figure.

StageTiming
Service on tenantAt least 4 days before trial
Hearing date10 to 21 days after filing
Jury demandAt least 3 days before trial
Appeal to county courtWithin 5 days of judgment
Writ of possession available6 days after final judgment
Writ served by officerWithin 5 days

Can a tenant appeal an eviction judgment?

Yes, but quickly. The county court appeal must be filed inside five days of judgment, and the tenant posts a bond or cash deposit or swears they cannot afford the costs.

A landlord who wins should know a timely appeal delays the writ. A tenant who misses the five-day window usually loses the right to appeal, so the clerk's office should be contacted right after judgment.

How a writ of possession works

Think of the writ as the court's permission slip for an officer to remove the tenant. Six days after final judgment it becomes available. Service happens within five days, followed by 24 hours of notice ahead of removal.

There are outer limits as well. A writ generally cannot issue more than 60 days after judgment, though the court may allow 90 days for good cause, and it cannot be carried out after the 90th day. A landlord who waits too long may have to go back to the court.

  • Day 6 after final judgment: the writ can be requested.
  • Within 5 days of that: the officer serves the writ.
  • 24 hours: warning before removal.
  • Day 90: last day to carry the writ out.

Squatters and occupants who are not tenants

Someone who never held a lease is not handled in justice court. Under Property Code chapter 24B, the owner files a request for removal with the sheriff or constable, and a lawsuit is unnecessary if the conditions are met.

  • The occupant stayed after being told to leave.
  • The property was not open to the public at entry.
  • No suit is pending between owner and occupant.
  • The occupant is not a family member or a current or former tenant.

A wrongful removal exposes the owner to a suit under section 24B.005. Section 24.0051606 adds a summary disposition path in forcible entry and detainer suits, with a four-day response and a trial 10 to 21 days after filing if the matter is disputed.

What to bring to the hearing

Expect the judge to check the notice first and the grounds second. Take the lease, the notice to vacate, proof of the delivery method and date, and the rent ledger.

  • The signed lease and any addenda.
  • The notice and delivery record, such as mail receipts or e-mail headers.
  • A ledger showing what was paid and what was missed.
  • Photos or letters connected to any lease violation.

A landlord who cannot show proper notice may have to refile, and the clocks above start over.

If the tenant leaves before judgment

Many cases end early. A tenant who moves out after the notice or after the suit is filed saves everyone the remaining steps. Get the keys back in writing and note the date.

If a signed move-out agreement exists, hold on to it with the lease and ledger. Ask the justice court clerk how to dismiss a pending case so the file closes cleanly.

A realistic timeline

Stack the stages and a simple case needs the notice period, up to three weeks to reach a hearing, and about a week after judgment before a writ can be served. An appeal or a reset hearing adds more.

The pieces are the 3-day default notice, the 10 to 21 day hearing window, the 5-day appeal period, the 6-day wait for the writ, the 5-day service period and the 24-hour removal warning. They are separate deadlines, so confirm each date in the court file.

Owners planning a sale should treat any single estimate as a rough guide. A buyer who will take the home with the tenant in it takes this uncertainty out of the closing schedule.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens at the hearing

Hearings are brief. Both sides speak, and the judge rules on who is entitled to possession. Only possession and, if joined, rent are at issue, so other disputes between the parties stay outside the case.

If the landlord wins, a judgment for possession is entered and the five-day appeal period starts. If the tenant wins, the case ends and the lease continues unless the landlord starts over with a new notice.

Eviction and selling a Texas rental

A sale can go ahead during an eviction, though pinning down a closing date is harder. A buyer who accepts the occupied house skips the court calendar entirely. A buyer who wants it vacant depends on the writ steps above.

Owners weighing a sale often ask three questions: does the lease pass to the buyer, is back rent still owed to the seller, and must the judgment be final before closing? Put the answers in the purchase contract, and keep the court file handy for the title company.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Texas eviction take?

No one number fits every case. Count about three days of notice, a hearing 10 to 21 days after filing, and a writ no earlier than day six after judgment. An appeal or a rescheduled hearing lengthens it.

Do I need a lawyer to file an eviction in justice court?

The procedure does not require a written answer from the tenant, and the case is built so people can handle it themselves. Ask the justice court clerk about local practice.

How fast must a tenant appeal an eviction?

Within five days of judgment, by filing a bond, a cash deposit or a statement of inability to afford costs with the county court.

How late can a writ be carried out?

On the 90th day after judgment at the latest. A writ normally cannot issue more than 60 days after judgment, and the court may allow 90 days for good cause.

Can a landlord change the locks to remove a tenant?

The lawful route is a court judgment and a writ carried out by an officer. Ask the justice court clerk or an attorney before taking any self-help step.

A Texas affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement of a decedent's family history that is recorded in the county deed records, and under Estates Code Sec. 203.001 a court treats it as prima facie evidence of the facts once it has been of record for five years. Read this guide before relying on one to sell a house.

Inherited a Texas house?

What an affidavit of heirship does in Texas

An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement about who a dead person's relatives were, recorded in the county deed records so that later readers of the title can see it. It records facts. It does not hand title to anyone by itself.

Estates Code Sec. 203.001 gives the document a specific evidentiary job. A court must treat a recorded statement of family history, marital status or the identity of heirs as prima facie evidence when it sits in a properly sworn or acknowledged instrument and has been of record for five years or more. The five years run in the deed records of the county where the land sits, or of the county where the decedent lived. If the statement has an error, anyone interested can prove the true facts, and the affidavit does not cut off an omitted heir or a creditor.

For a seller, the buyer's side decides whether it trusts the affidavit. It is a sworn statement that no court has verified, and no law forces a third party to accept it.

What the statutory form contains

Section 203.002 prints a model form, and an affidavit that follows it substantially is the safest starting point. The form asks the person signing to describe how they know the family and then to list facts in numbered paragraphs.

  • Who the affiant is, where they live, and how long they knew the decedent.
  • The decedent's date and place of death and last residence.
  • The decedent's marital history, with the date and place of a spouse's death if the spouse died first.
  • Each child, with birth date, the other parent and current address, or the date of death and descendants of a child who died.
  • Whether the decedent had a will, whether any administration took place, and whether debts or estate taxes remain unpaid.
  • The real property the decedent owned an interest in, to the best of the affiant's knowledge.

The form closes with a signature and a notary's jurat. Paragraphs for parents and siblings apply only when no descendants survived, so the right version depends on the family. A title company reading the affidavit will look for gaps in the children paragraph first, because an unlisted child is the classic way these documents fail.

Who inherits when there is no will

Estates Code ch. 201 sets the order. The affidavit has to match this order, so read the rules before anyone signs.

With no spouse, the estate goes to children and their descendants. If no child line survives, it goes in equal shares to the father and mother, and then to siblings and their descendants when a parent is gone. With a surviving spouse, the statute splits the estate into separate property and community property. The community estate passes entirely to the surviving spouse when the decedent left no descendants, or when every surviving child is also the spouse's child. If a child of another relationship survives, the decedent's undivided half of the community passes to that child line.

Separate real estate follows a different formula. With children, the spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the land and the children take the remainder. With no children, the spouse takes half of the land outright and the rest passes under the descent rules. These splits are why a house owned by a long-married couple can produce an affidavit very different from a house the decedent owned before marriage.

Is an affidavit enough to close a sale?

Sometimes, but the outcome rests on the buyer and the title company, not on the statute. The affidavit proves family facts. A title insurer still has to accept those facts and insure the buyer against a missing heir.

Section 201.053 offers protection that matters here. A buyer who pays value and relies in good faith on an affidavit that omits a child who was not a presumed child, and who has no knowledge of that child's claim, still gets good title to the interest. The omitted child can pursue the heirs for sale proceeds, so the risk shifts to the family rather than the purchaser. Ownership claims by undisclosed or missing heirs count as title defects, which explains why insurers scrutinize these papers.

Expect a title company to ask for a recorded affidavit, a death certificate, and often a signature from every heir at closing. If anyone refuses, or if the heirs cannot be located, a court-based route is usually cleaner.

Other ways to clear title to inherited property

Several routes exist, and the right choice turns on whether a will exists, whether debts need handling, and whether anyone contests who the heirs are.

Routes for passing a Texas decedent's real property
RouteCourt order neededDocument filed with the clerk
Affidavit of heirshipNoSworn affidavit in the deed records
Muniment of titleYesCourt order and the will
Administered estateYesExecutor's or administrator's deed
Transfer on death deedNoDeed filed before death, then an affidavit of death and the death certificate
Determination of heirshipYesCourt judgment naming the heirs

A clerk cannot add heirs to the old deed afterward, so choose the route before the listing goes live.

Property tax and homestead after a death

The tax bill keeps coming, and the heirs must deal with it. Bills become delinquent on a set schedule with penalties, so ask the county tax office for the dates.

Heirs living in the house may also qualify for an exemption. Anyone not named on a recorded deed must give the appraisal district a sworn statement of ownership interest, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. A recorded heirship affidavit can support the ownership paperwork.

Get the current balance from the county tax assessor-collector before accepting an offer.

Federal tax when heirs sell

Basis for inherited property comes from Publication 551 rather than from the purchase price, so heirs should pull that publication before they compute any gain. Basis normally means cost, but property acquired by gift or inheritance follows separate rules.

If the house sells, Form 1099-S may be issued, and a sale must be reported when you receive that form even if the gain is excludable. Texas has no state income tax. A CPA can tell you how basis, holding period and the home-sale exclusion apply to your particular heirs.

A cash sale lets the heirs close without waiting on a buyer's loan approval, which helps when several relatives live in different places and must each sign.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Texas affidavit of heirship the same as a deed?

No. A deed conveys title. An affidavit states family facts and is recorded in the county deed records. Under Estates Code Sec. 203.001 it becomes prima facie evidence in court after five years of record, but it does not transfer ownership.

Who can sign an affidavit of heirship?

The statutory form calls for an affiant with personal knowledge of the decedent's family and marital history, signing before a notary. The form's optional paragraph also lets the affiant name others who know the family. Title companies often prefer someone who is not an heir.

Does a title company have to accept one?

No. Nothing in the law forces a third party to accept it. Whether a title insurer will cover a buyer depends on how complete the affidavit looks and whether any heir is missing or disputes the facts.

What if the affidavit leaves out a child?

A good-faith buyer who pays value and does not know of the child's claim can keep good title under Estates Code Sec. 201.053, but the omitted child may pursue the heirs for sale proceeds. The error can also delay a closing while the title company sorts it out.

Where is the affidavit recorded?

At the county clerk's office, which keeps the deed records for the property's county. An instrument must be signed and acknowledged or sworn before an authorized officer. Ask the clerk for current fees.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Texas small estate affidavit lets the heirs of someone who died without a will collect the estate without a personal representative, if the estate assets other than the homestead and exempt property are worth $75,000 or less. The rules are in Estates Code Chapter 205. A judge must approve the affidavit, and it can transfer title to real estate only in one case: the decedent's homestead when it is the only real property in the estate.

Inherited a house through a small estate?
We buy inherited houses as-is with no repairs, no agent commission and a closing date you choose.

What a small estate affidavit is

A small estate affidavit is a sworn court filing under Chapter 205 of the Estates Code. It lets heirs collect or transfer a modest estate without a full administration, and it fits people who died with no will and a small estate.

It sits among the informal probate methods, next to the affidavit of heirship and the order of no administration. Because a judge must approve it, banks and agencies give it more weight than a sworn statement that is only filed with a clerk. For anyone hoping to sell a Texas house after a death, the first question is whether this tool reaches real estate at all. The answer is narrow.

Requirements

The estate must have no will, no pending application for administration, and countable assets capped at $75,000. The $75,000 figure leaves out the homestead and exempt property.

The estate also needs enough assets to pay its debts, and all the heirs must agree. The affidavit is sworn by two disinterested witnesses, the death must be at least 30 days in the past, and no petition for a personal representative can be pending or already granted.

  • The person died intestate, meaning without a will.
  • The asset total is $75,000 or under, excluding the homestead and exempt property.
  • No application for administration has been filed.
  • The estate can pay its debts.
  • Every heir agrees to the affidavit.
  • The court approves it.

Does it let heirs sell a Texas house?

Generally no. The estate cannot include real property, with one exception: a homestead that passes to the surviving spouse or minor children.

When that exception applies, the clerk where the homestead is located records a copy of the approved affidavit, and title underwriters will want to see that recorded copy. An heir who inherits an ordinary rental house, a vacant lot or a second property needs a different route, covered below.

If you are in a hurry to close, talk with the title company before you sign anything. They decide which recorded documents they will insure, and that can differ from what a family expects. Even when the affidavit is available, compare it with the cost and timing of a full probate before choosing.

Other ways to transfer inherited real estate

The right document depends on whether there is a will, whether the estate was administered, and whether the owner signed a TOD deed. Each situation has its own paperwork to record.

Recorded paperwork by situation
SituationWhat gets recorded
Owner signed a TOD deedAffidavit of death and the death certificate
Estate administered by a personal representativeExecutor's or administrator's deed
Will with no debts besides real estate liens (muniment of title)Court order and the will
OtherwiseAffidavit of heirship

The county cannot simply add heirs to the old deed. A new instrument has to be recorded.

How an affidavit of heirship differs

The affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement of who the heirs are. It is filed at the clerk's office without any judge reviewing it, and no law forces a buyer, bank or title insurer to accept it.

That makes it a weaker tool than a small estate affidavit even when it is easier to file. A determination of heirship and an order of no administration are the other routes when a title company wants court backing. If the family expects to sell soon, ask the buyer's title company early which one they will accept.

How long do heirs have to probate a will?

Four years from the death is the usual window to offer a will, and a court can accept a late filing with an acceptable reason. File the application with the probate court covering the decedent's last home.

A valid will is written, signed and witnessed by two people, while a holographic will needs no witnesses. A muniment of title can move property without administration when a will exists and the only debts are real estate liens. Both documents are filed where the land lies.

Where to file and what the clerk does

Probate filings, including applications and small estate affidavits, go through the county clerk, who also records deeds and notices. The clerk is the county recorder, which is why recorded transfer paperwork ends up there too.

  • Small estate affidavits and probate applications: filed with the probate court that covers the decedent's residence.
  • Homestead copies of an approved affidavit: recorded at the clerk's office for the home's county.
  • Deeds, orders and affidavits of heirship: recorded in the land's own county.

The clerk accepts a land conveyance for recording only when it is acknowledged before an authorized officer or sworn before two subscribing witnesses. Call the clerk's office for the fee total before you go.

Inherited homestead and the tax exemption

Heirs who are not on the recorded deed must show the appraisal district proof of their interest. The Comptroller's exemptions page lists the exact documents.

A buyer who takes the home after January 1 can sometimes claim the exemption at once for the rest of that year, if the previous owner never received it. Ask the appraisal district how much of the homestead exemption applies in your school district. Surviving spouses aged 55 and up may keep a late spouse's senior exemption in some cases.

Can a TOD deed avoid the whole process?

It can, if the owner signed and recorded it before death. Real estate passes to the named beneficiary outside probate. Charities may be named, and the owner can cancel the deed.

The owner has to record it while still alive, at the clerk's office for the land's county. A Lady Bird deed (an enhanced life estate) lets the owner sell or mortgage without the beneficiary's approval, and no official form exists for it. Families who learn that an older relative signed one should locate the recorded copy with the clerk before anything else.

Where no such deed exists and the estate does not qualify for the small estate route, a family can still sell after a court order, an executor's deed or another recorded instrument supports the title. Leave room in the schedule for those steps when picking a closing date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the title company

Whichever route applies, a buyer's title company will ask for the same basics. Gather certified copies of the death certificate, the recorded deed into the decedent, any court order or approved affidavit, and a list of the heirs with their contact details.

Ask early whether the title company wants anything else recorded before closing. A short call can save weeks. A cash buyer also skips the lender's underwriting, though the title company still insists on a clean recorded chain, so the paperwork above is needed either way.

Frequently asked questions

What is the dollar limit for a Texas small estate affidavit?

$75,000 in assets, not counting the homestead or exempt property. The estate must also be able to pay its debts, and all heirs must agree.

Does a small estate affidavit work if there is a will?

No. The procedure is for estates without a will. With a will, the usual options are probate or a muniment of title, which the court approves.

Can I sell inherited land using a small estate affidavit?

Usually not. The affidavit cannot cover real property other than a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children, so other heirs typically need probate, a recorded deed or another court-backed route.

How long after death can the affidavit be filed?

At least 30 days must pass after the death before the affidavit is made. Ask the probate court clerk about any other timing the court applies.

Will a title company accept an affidavit of heirship?

Not automatically. No law forces anyone to accept it, so confirm with the title company before listing.

The Texas Comptroller's history of state taxes says S.B. 752 repealed Tax Code Chapter 211 and did not affect tax that accrued before that date. Federal estate tax still exists, but returns are required only for estates above a filing threshold that the IRS lists at $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

Does Texas tax inheritances or estates?

Not anymore. Texas repealed its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752 (2015), effective September 1, 2015, which removed Tax Code Chapter 211.

The federal estate tax is the main death tax an heir hears about, and it reaches only large estates. For the heirs of a Texas house, the everyday issues are property tax, probate paperwork and recording the deed, all covered below.

When the federal estate tax applies

Form 706 comes into play only when the gross estate, adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption add up to more than the filing threshold for the year of death. Plain estates of cash, public securities and a few easily valued assets typically need no return.

Federal estate tax return filing thresholds by year of death
Year of deathFiling threshold
2020$11,580,000
2021$11,700,000
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Those amounts are filing triggers, not rates. For the estate, the house is valued at what it was worth on the date of death, not what the owner paid, and mortgages, debts, administration costs and gifts to a spouse or qualified charity come off the total. Spouses can elect portability of unused exemption by filing on time.

How the estate tax is figured

Federal tax is worked out in steps, and your house is just one line in the math. Texas estates use the same method as every other state.

  • Gross estate: everything owned or partly controlled at death, at fair market value. Cash, securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities and business interests all count.
  • Taxable estate: the gross estate minus allowed deductions such as debts, administration costs and bequests to a surviving spouse or qualified charity. Some operating businesses and farms may be valued lower if they qualify.
  • Lifetime gifts: taxable gifts made since 1977 are added before the tax is computed.
  • Credit: the tax is then reduced by the available unified credit.

Because mortgages are deductible, a heavily financed house counts for less than its market price. Spouses sometimes file even when no tax is due, because the return is how a surviving spouse claims the unused exemption through portability. If you are unsure whether a Form 706 applies, ask a tax professional, since the test counts gifts as well as the estate.

How the federal threshold has changed

The big jump came in 2018. For deaths in 2017 the IRS table lists $5,490,000, and for 2018 it lists $11,180,000. It has risen every year since, to $11,400,000 for 2019, $13,610,000 for 2024 and $15,000,000 for 2026.

Earlier years run from $5,000,000 for 2011 up through $5,450,000 for 2016. If your family read about the old limits, those numbers may no longer apply. Match the year of death to the IRS table before deciding whether a return is needed. The table also covers 2012 through 2015 for an older death.

How a Texas house passes to heirs

Which route fits depends on two things: whether a will exists and whether a judge has to oversee the process. Every route leaves a trail in the county clerk's records.

  • Probating a will: the application is due within four years of death, though a court may take a late one for good cause.
  • Muniment of title: suits an estate whose only debts are liens on the land. The order and the will get filed in the county of the land.
  • Small estate affidavit (Estates Code Chapter 205): a court-approved shortcut for estates at or under $75,000 before homestead and exempt property.
  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement left with the clerk. No law makes a buyer or lender accept it.
  • Transfer on death deed: moves land outside probate if recorded while the owner is alive.

Small estate affidavit requirements

The conditions are no will, no administration underway, enough assets to cover debts, and every heir in agreement. A judge must sign off.

This shortcut cannot carry real property unless it is a homestead going to a spouse or minor children. It also requires two disinterested witnesses, a waiting month after death, and no pending or granted petition for a personal representative. The homestead copy goes on record.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which deed an heir needs to sell

Each route produces a different document, and the title company asks for the one that matches.

  • Transfer on death deed: a recorded affidavit of death with the certificate.
  • Administered estate: the executor's or administrator's deed.
  • Muniment of title: the order plus the will.
  • No court action: an affidavit of heirship.

A county will not rewrite the old deed to add heirs. The recorded instrument is what carries title forward. Ask the clerk what it charges to record.

Property tax on an inherited house

Probate does not pause the tax clock. On every January 1 a lien attaches for that year's taxes, penalties and interest, regardless of who ends up with title.

  • Billing starts around October 1 and delinquency begins February 1.
  • Late charges begin the day after January 31, and the penalty climbs through the summer.
  • If an heir is missing from the recorded deed, the exemption claim still works with four papers: an ownership affidavit, the death certificate, a utility bill and any court record citation.
  • In some cases a surviving spouse aged 55 or older inherits the over-65 exemption.

An heir who keeps the house and qualifies also gets the yearly appraisal cap on homesteads.

What makes a will valid for probate?

Expect a will to be written, signed and witnessed. A will in the maker's own handwriting, called holographic, needs no witnesses.

The probate court for the decedent's home county usually takes the application. A different tool, the enhanced life estate deed (called a Lady Bird deed), lets the owner keep full power to sell or borrow, although no official form exists.

First steps for heirs of a Texas house

Find out which route the estate will take, because that decides which document the title company needs. Locate any will, the death certificate and the latest deed.

  • Phone the appraisal district to learn what exemption the house carries now and whether a fresh application is due.
  • Find out from the county tax office if this year's bill is paid and what a payoff would cost.
  • Get from the county clerk a list of everything recorded against the property, liens included.
  • Keep the house insured and the utilities on while title is sorted out.

If the estate is large enough that the federal threshold might matter, bring in an accountant early, since the tax test counts lifetime gifts along with the house.

Selling an inherited house

At closing, the sale price pays the mortgage, tax and recorded liens first, and the heirs share what is left under whatever route governs the estate. Line up the recorded deed, payoffs and tax statement before you accept an offer.

Federal rules govern income tax on a gain and gift tax, and a tax professional can answer those. Locally, ask the tax office for a payoff and the clerk for copies of what is recorded. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval, though the title paperwork above is still required.

Frequently asked questions

Is there still a Texas inheritance tax?

There is none today. A 2015 law, Senate Bill 752, wiped out the state inheritance tax in Tax Code Chapter 211 beginning September 1, 2015.

At what estate size does a 2026 death trigger a federal return?

The figure is $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths, compared with $13,990,000 for 2025. Cross that line and a return is required; it is not a tax percentage.

Who pays the tax bill on a house that came through an estate?

Yes. The yearly lien sticks to the property on January 1, so the bill follows the house to whoever holds title.

How long after a death can a will be probated?

Generally four years after the death. After that, a court may still accept the application if it finds a good reason.

Is probate always needed before an heir can sell?

Sometimes. If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed in life, probate is avoided, and simpler estates may use a muniment of title or small estate affidavit. Your title company has the final say on what it will insure.

A Texas warranty deed conveys real estate with a covenant of general warranty, meaning the seller promises to defend the buyer's title against anyone lawfully claiming it. Property Code Sec. 5.022 gives a statutory form for it. Texas statutes do not use the names "general warranty deed" or "special warranty deed," so this guide sticks to what the code says.

Ready to sell your Texas house?
We buy as-is, close with your title company and pay no agent commission.

What a warranty deed is in Texas

A Texas warranty deed is a written conveyance of real estate in which the seller also promises to defend the title against other claims. The statutory model form in Property Code Section 5.022 conveys a fee simple estate with a covenant of general warranty.

Under Section 5.021, any conveyance of a freehold or an estate for more than one year must be in writing, signed by the seller or the seller's authorized agent, and delivered. Handshake sales and emailed promises do not move title to a house.

The statutory form

The form names the seller and buyer, states the price paid, grants and conveys the described property, and ends with a promise to warrant and defend it. The language in Section 5.022(a) binds the seller, and the seller's heirs, executors and administrators, to defend the premises against every person lawfully claiming any part of it.

  • County and state of signing.
  • The names and places of residence of both sides.
  • The sale price recited as consideration.
  • A description of the premises.
  • The habendum clause (to have and to hold), with the buyer and the buyer's heirs or assigns.
  • The warranty paragraph and the seller's signature.

A covenant of warranty is not required in a conveyance, and the parties may use any form or clause that does not violate the law. A seller can therefore use a shorter or different deed, which is why a title company reads every deed before closing.

What the word convey promises on its own

Even without express warranty language, using "grant" or "convey" in a fee simple deed implies two limited promises under Section 5.023. The seller says the estate has not been conveyed to anyone else before, and that at signing the estate has no encumbrances.

Section 5.024 defines an encumbrance to include a tax, an assessment and a lien on real property. A buyer can sue on an implied covenant just as if it were written into the deed, unless the deed expressly provides otherwise. That makes an unpaid tax bill or a forgotten lien a potential warranty problem for the seller, which is one more reason to run payoff figures before closing.

Warranty deed versus title insurance

A deed warranty is not a substitute for a title search. It is a personal promise from the seller, which is only as good as the seller's willingness and ability to honor it years later.

Buyers who want protection beyond the seller's word commonly ask for a title commitment before closing. For a seller, the takeaway is practical: a general warranty exposes you to claims about defects you did not cause, so ask the title company to flag recorded liens, unreleased mortgages, back taxes and gaps in the chain before you sign.

  • Unpaid property tax is an encumbrance under Section 5.024.
  • A mortgage still of record at the time of signing is a lien on the estate.
  • An unrecorded earlier deed to someone else would break the promise implied by the word convey.

General or special warranty: which one does a seller sign?

The deed that matches your contract is the right one, and the contract usually says. A general warranty deed protects the buyer against defects from any time in the chain. A special warranty deed words the promise more narrowly, so the two forms differ in how far the seller's duty reaches.

Ask the title company or an attorney how each form is worded and what it covers. Because the statute allows parties to use any lawful clause, sellers and buyers negotiate this before signing. If you are selling a house that came to you by inheritance or a recent foreclosure, ask your title company which form the buyer expects.

Who may sign a deed for the owner

Section 5.021 allows the seller's agent to sign if the agent is authorized in writing. A verbal authorization will not satisfy the statute for a sale of land.

That is why a sale by an attorney in fact, an executor or a trustee comes with paperwork: a recorded power of attorney or court letters that the clerk and title company can read. If the person selling the house is acting for someone else, gather those documents early, because a missing authorization is a common reason a closing is pushed back.

Signing and recording the deed

The deed has to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses, before the county clerk will record it. Property Code Section 12.001(b) sets that rule, and the clerk records deeds in the county where the property is located.

Recording fees vary by county, so use the clerk's current schedule. Travis County, for one, charges $25.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page, plus $0.25 for each name indexed over five, and a $20.00 or double-fee penalty when the grantee's mailing address is missing. Other counties set their own amounts.

Fixing an error in a recorded deed

File a correction instrument. Sections 5.027 to 5.030 allow a recorded deed to be corrected for an ambiguity or error, including one in the legal description.

Which kind you need depends on the error:

  • Nonmaterial changes (Section 5.028): a person with personal knowledge of the facts can prepare and sign the instrument to fix clerical mistakes such as a wrong lot or block number, a misspelled name, a wrong date of signing or the marital status of a party.
  • Material changes (Section 5.029): the parties to the original deal, or their heirs, successors or assigns, must all sign to add or remove land, or to add a mortgagee's consent. The instrument must be recorded in every county where the original deed is recorded.

A valid correction takes effect as of the original deed's date, is presumed true, and puts later buyers on notice (Section 5.030). It does not beat the rights of a creditor or a later buyer for value without notice who acquired their interest before the correction was recorded.

Discriminatory wording in an old deed

Section 5.026 makes any restriction or deed provision that bars use, sale or transfer because of race, color, religion or national origin void, and a court must dismiss suits to enforce it.

Under Section 5.0261, the owner of property whose chain of title includes such wording, or someone with the owner's permission, can ask a court to remove the provision by filing a verified motion with the district clerk in the county where the instrument is recorded. Many older Texas subdivisions have this language in recorded covenants, and it often turns up when a title company searches before a sale.

What a seller should check before signing

Confirm the deed matches the contract, the legal description matches the survey and the prior deed, and the names match everyone who holds title. A final review by the title company or an attorney is worth the time because a deed cannot be cleanly undone once it is recorded.

  • Spell every owner's name as it appears on the vesting deed.
  • Confirm the type of warranty the contract calls for.
  • Get payoff letters for mortgages and any tax liens.
  • Bring identification for the notary.
  • Ask the county clerk where the original must be delivered, since Travis County, for example, wants originals rather than copies.

Frequently asked questions

Is a warranty deed required to sell a house in Texas?

No. A covenant of warranty is optional under Property Code Section 5.022(b). Any signed, delivered written conveyance can pass title, but buyers and lenders commonly ask for a warranty deed, so check what your contract requires.

Does a Texas warranty deed need to be notarized?

Yes, to be recorded. Section 12.001(b) of the Property Code requires acknowledgment before an authorized officer such as a notary, or proof by two subscribing witnesses, before the county clerk can record a deed to real property.

What does the word convey imply in a Texas deed?

It implies two promises: the seller has not already conveyed the property to someone else, and the property is free from encumbrances at signing. Section 5.023 allows a lawsuit on those implied covenants unless the deed says otherwise.

How do I fix a wrong lot number in my deed?

File a nonmaterial correction instrument under Section 5.028, signed by a person with personal knowledge of the facts. Record it in the county where the deed was recorded, and ask the clerk about the current fee.

Where do I record a Texas deed?

With the county clerk of the county where the land sits. Fees differ by county, and some clerks, like Travis County, require the original signed document rather than a copy.

What a quitclaim deed is, and where it fits

A quitclaim deed is one of several deed types the county clerk records in Texas, alongside general warranty, special warranty, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds. It is filed in the deed records at the clerk's office covering the land.

A quitclaim passes whatever interest the signer has, if any, and promises nothing more. How much comfort that gives a buyer is a question for a title company or a Texas real estate attorney, so ask before you rely on anyone's promise about it.

For a seller the practical point is simple. A buyer's title company reads every deed in the chain, and a quitclaim anywhere in that chain can prompt extra questions. The sooner you know what is in your own chain of title, the fewer surprises appear after you sign a sale contract.

What else the county clerk handles

Several of the clerk's jobs touch a sale. The same office records deeds, deeds of trust, liens and foreclosure sale notices, serves the commissioners court, and accepts probate filings such as applications and small estate affidavits.

A single call can tell you whether a deed, a lien or a probate filing is on record against your property. State tax lien notices from the Comptroller land there as well and go into the state tax lien book. Ask for copies of anything indexed under your name and the prior owner's before you tell a buyer the title is clean.

  • Deed records for every type of conveyance named above.
  • Releases of liens, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney.
  • Probate filings and small estate affidavits.

What a deed needs before the clerk will record it

The grantor signs, and the deed then needs either an acknowledgment before an officer who can take one, a sworn statement, or the signatures of two subscribing witnesses. This is the rule in Property Code 12.001(b). A notary, a county clerk, a district clerk or a county court judge can take an acknowledgment.

  • Signature by the person giving up the interest.
  • An acknowledgment or sworn statement, or two subscribing witnesses.
  • Filing in the clerk's office for the county that covers the land.
  • The recording fees the clerk charges, listed below.

Recording puts your interest in the public record. An unfiled deed in a drawer is invisible to the next buyer or lender who searches.

What the clerk charges to file a deed

Expect a modest per-page charge with several smaller add-ons. The clerk's posted schedule is the one that counts, so call before you file.

Leave off the grantee's mailing address and the clerk can add $25.

Can a quitclaim deed move a house out of an estate?

Normally an estate house leaves through the probate paperwork, and one heir's quitclaim does not replace it. The recorded paper depends on how the owner left the property.

  • A recorded affidavit of death and a death certificate go with a transfer on death deed.
  • An estate under administration uses a deed from its executor or administrator.
  • A will proved as a muniment of title relies on the court order.
  • Without any of those, an affidavit of heirship may be used.

Nobody at the county can add heirs to the old deed, though an heir can ask the clerk what is on file. An affidavit of heirship is sworn but never checked by a court, and third parties need not accept it.

Transfer on death deeds and Lady Bird deeds

Families sometimes consider these before signing a quitclaim over to a relative. A transfer on death deed skips probate, may name a charity as beneficiary, can be revoked by the owner, and has to be on record with the clerk before the owner dies.

The Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate deed, lets the owner sell or mortgage without the beneficiary's consent. No official form exists for it. Because these deeds shape what a buyer can purchase later, a title company usually wants to see them before closing.

Taxes and liens that travel with a deed

Each January 1 a lien attaches to secure that year's property taxes, and it lets a court foreclose even after the title changes hands. Whoever held title on that date owes the year's bill and can be sued for it after selling.

Delinquent taxes block clean title for a buyer. Giving the house away by quitclaim does not wipe out that lien, so the tax office should confirm each year's status before any listing or transfer.

How a quitclaim shows up in a title search

Examiners trace ownership backward, deed by deed, until the chain reaches a solid starting point. A quitclaim is a link that says the signer gave up whatever claim he or she had. It makes no promise that the claim was good. If an earlier owner never had full title, nothing in the quitclaim fixes that.

That is why a family transfer between spouses, siblings or parents and children can look fine for years and then draw questions at the first sale. The examiner may ask for the missing deed, an heir's signature, a tax statement or a corrective instrument before agreeing to insure the buyer. None of this is unusual, and it goes faster when you start before a buyer is waiting. Keep copies of every deed and tax statement you gather in one folder, so the title company and your attorney can work from the same set.

Selling a house you hold by quitclaim

Order a title search or call a title company early, and read each deed in your chain of title. Quitclaims, handwritten deeds, missing signatures and unrecorded transfers are the items that slow a closing.

  • Pull the recorded deeds from the county clerk and check each one for a signature and an acknowledgment.
  • Check whether every co-owner or heir signed.
  • Get a tax status statement for every year from the county tax office.
  • Find out from the title company what it requires before it will insure a buyer.

Bring the chain, the tax statements and any probate paper to your first call with the title company so it can tell you in one pass what is missing.

If the chain has gaps that the title company cannot clear, a Texas real estate attorney can say whether a corrective instrument or a court action is the right fix. A cash buyer will still want the chain to read cleanly, though with no lender in the deal the closing is often quicker once the gaps are repaired.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed filed at the clerk's office in Texas?

Yes. Quitclaim deeds are recorded in the deed records at the clerk covering the real property, after the deed is signed and acknowledged or witnessed.

What does recording a Texas deed cost?

The 2023 schedule itemizes a charge per page, two records fees capped at $10 each and a $2.00 technology fee. Your clerk can quote the current total.

Can a quitclaim deed stop probate?

No. Inherited real property moves through a transfer on death deed, a muniment of title, an administered-estate deed or an affidavit of heirship. Ask the clerk or a probate attorney before relying on a quitclaim.

Will a quitclaim erase unpaid property taxes?

No. The January 1 tax lien lets a court foreclose even after ownership changes, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid.

Who can say whether my quitclaim will pass title insurance?

A title company or a Texas attorney. Each underwriter has its own requirements, so ask before you list.

A muniment of title is a Texas court order that admits a will to probate only to prove who owns the property, without opening a full estate administration. It is available when the estate owes no debt other than debt secured by a lien on real estate, or when the court finds some other reason administration is unnecessary. The rules are in Estates Code Chapter 257.

What a muniment of title is

A muniment of title is a court order that admits a will to probate without naming an executor to run the estate. It lets the people named in the will deal with the property as if the record title were already in their names.

Under Estates Code Sec. 257.102, the order gives banks, transfer agents and anyone holding estate assets enough authority to pay or transfer them without administration. For a house, the result is a recorded order and will that connect the dead owner to the people who inherit.

When a court can admit a will this way

Sec. 257.001 allows it in two situations. Either the estate owes no unpaid debt other than a debt secured by a lien on real estate, or the court finds some other reason that administration is unnecessary.

The real estate lien carve out is what makes the route workable for house owners: a mortgage does not block a muniment. Other debts do. A credit card balance, a medical bill or a tax debt can push the family toward full administration instead. The route is common when the only asset passing under the will is real property.

What the applicant must prove

The application is filed in the probate court, usually in the county where the owner lived. Under Sec. 257.054 the applicant has to prove each of these to the court's satisfaction.

  • The owner is dead.
  • Four years have not passed between the date of death and the filing.
  • The court has jurisdiction and venue, and citation was served and returned as the code requires.
  • The estate owes no unpaid debt apart from real estate liens, or administration is unnecessary for another reason.
  • The owner did not revoke the will.
  • If the will is not self-proved, the owner signed it with the required formalities, was of sound mind, and was an adult, or was or had been married, or served in the armed forces.

Sec. 257.051 sets the contents of the application: the applicant, the owner's details, a general description of the property and its probable value, the will date, the executor named in the will, any witnesses, whether a child was born or adopted after the will was signed, whether a marriage ended after the will was made, and whether the state or a charity is a devisee.
