Muniment of titleYesNoCourt order and copy of the will, with the county clerk where the property sits
Probate with administrationUsuallyYes, appointed by the courtExecutor's or administrator's deed
Affidavit of heirshipNoNoSworn affidavit with the county clerk, which a third party is not required to accept
Transfer on death deedNoNoDeed recorded before the owner's death, plus an affidavit of death and the death certificate

How soon must someone act?

The will must be filed within four years of the death. A court can sometimes accept a will after that period if the applicant shows an acceptable reason for the delay. Sec. 257.054 still asks the applicant to prove the four years had not run, so waiting is a real risk.

After the will is admitted, the applicant has until the 180th day to file a sworn affidavit with the court clerk stating which terms of the will have been carried out and which have not (Sec. 257.103). The court can waive the report or extend the time. Missing it does not undo title passing under the will.

What the order does for a house sale

The order and the will go to the county clerk in the county where the house stands, which builds the chain of title from the owner to the beneficiary. A beneficiary under the will is then entitled to deal with the property as if title were already recorded in the beneficiary's name (Sec. 257.102(b)).

Sec. 257.101 also lets the court add a declaratory judgment to the order, either to interpret an unclear will or to name who takes when the will leaves that open. That judgment is conclusive against an omitted person in a dispute with a good faith buyer who purchased after it was entered.

A few steps usually follow the order:

  • Pay the mortgage or arrange payoff at closing, since the muniment route allows real estate liens to remain.
  • Check the property tax account. Texas taxes attach as a lien on January 1, the bill date is October 1 and the delinquency date is February 1.
  • Ask the county clerk what the recording fee will be for the order and will. A base fee applies per page, and extra pages are priced separately.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who should handle the filing?

Beneficiaries will likely need an attorney to file the application. Some counties also have their own probate court rules and forms, so call the probate clerk in the county where the owner lived before preparing papers.

If the family expects a dispute over the will, or the estate owes unsecured debts, plan for a different path. A muniment order does not fix a will contest and cannot clear debts that fall outside the real estate lien exception.

Which counties and courts are involved

Two places matter and they are often different. The application goes to the probate court, usually in the county where the owner lived. The order and will are then recorded with the county clerk in the county where the real property sits. That split matters when a family house stands in a different county from the owner's last address.

A county clerk also acts as the county recorder and as the clerk who holds probate filings. Under Sec. 257.052, a will filed with the application stays in the clerk's custody unless a court order removes it. A buyer can therefore ask the clerk for certified copies of the order and will to hand to the title company.

An instrument conveying real property can be recorded only if it is signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses or an authorized officer. When the beneficiary later sells, expect the new deed to need that acknowledgment, even though the muniment order itself already links the chain.

Common mistakes to avoid

Most problems come from the facts the statute asks the applicant to swear to. Check each before filing.

  • Assuming there are no debts, then finding an unsecured balance that blocks the route.
  • Waiting past the four year period after the death.
  • Leaving out a child born or adopted after the will was signed, which the application must address.
  • Forgetting that a marriage ended after the will was made, another item the application states.
  • Missing the 180 day report, which the court can waive or extend.

Before you list the house, line up the paper a buyer's title company will ask for: the recorded order, the will copy, the mortgage payoff and a current tax statement. A cash buyer can usually close on that file as soon as the order sits in the land records, since there is no lender underwriting it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can I use a muniment of title if the house has a mortgage?

Yes. Sec. 257.001 allows it when the only unpaid debts are secured by a lien on real estate. A mortgage fits that description, so the loan can stay in place or be paid off at closing.

Does a muniment of title name an executor?

No. The route is meant for estates that need no administration. Beneficiaries under the will deal with the property directly after the order is entered.

Is there a deadline to apply?

Yes. The applicant must show four years have not passed since the date of death. A court can sometimes accept a later filing for an acceptable reason, so talk to an attorney quickly.

What do I record to sell the house?

File the court order and a copy of the will with the county clerk in the county where the property sits. That recording links the owner to the beneficiary for the title company.

What if there is no will?

Then muniment of title is not available, because it needs a will. Look at the heirship affidavit, determination of heirship or administration routes instead.

When a Texas resident dies without a will, Estates Code Chapter 201 decides who inherits, and the answer depends on whether there is a spouse, children, parents or siblings and on whether the property is community or separate. This guide summarizes the statute's main rules. It does not cover homestead rights, which Chapter 201 does not address.

Who inherits a Texas house with no will?

Chapter 201 of the Estates Code lists the heirs in a fixed order, so the house goes to relatives by formula and not by what the family expects. The result turns on three things: whether the owner left a spouse, whether there are children, and whether the house was community property or separate property.

An heir becomes an owner the moment the owner dies, yet the county records still show the dead person as owner. Until heirs are proven by a court order or a recorded affidavit, a title company will usually refuse to insure a sale. That gap between owning and being able to sell is where many Texas families lose time.

A surviving spouse and children

The answer depends on the kind of property. The code treats the community estate separately from everything else.

For community property, the whole community estate goes to the surviving spouse when the deceased spouse had no descendants, or when every surviving child or grandchild is also a descendant of the surviving spouse (Sec. 201.003). If the owner had a child who is not also the surviving spouse's child, the owner's undivided half of the community estate goes to the owner's descendants instead, still charged with community debts.

For separate property, a surviving spouse with children in the picture takes one third of the personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. The children share the other two thirds of the personal property and hold the remainder interest in the land (Sec. 201.002(b)). When a life estate exists, ask a probate attorney who must sign before a buyer can get clean title.

How the shares divide

The table follows the statute for common family patterns. It does not cover every case, and "land" and "personal estate" are the code's own terms.

Texas intestate shares by family pattern (Estates Code 201.001 to 201.003)
Family situationWho takes
Spouse survives, community property, all children are also the spouse'sSurviving spouse takes the community estate
Spouse survives, community property, a child from another relationship existsThat child and other descendants take the deceased spouse's undivided half
Spouse and children survive, separate propertySpouse: one third of personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. Children: the rest
Spouse survives, no children, separate property, parent or sibling also survivesSpouse: all personal property and one half of the land. The other half of the land follows the kindred rules
Spouse survives, no children, no parent, no sibling or their descendantsSpouse takes the entire estate
No spouse, children surviveChildren and their descendants
No spouse, no descendants, both parents surviveEqual shares to father and mother

When there is no surviving spouse

With no spouse, the estate moves down a list of kindred set by Sec. 201.001. Children and their descendants come first and take everything.

  • No descendants, both parents alive: the parents split the estate equally.
  • No descendants, one parent alive: half to that parent and half to the siblings and their descendants, or all to the parent if there are no siblings or sibling descendants.
  • No descendants, no parents: siblings and their descendants.
  • None of those: the estate divides into two halves, one for paternal kindred and one for maternal kindred, working through grandparents and then their descendants.

When a child died before the owner, that child's own descendants step into the child's place. The code calls this per capita with representation (Sec. 201.101).

Adopted children, half siblings and late-born children

An adopted child inherits from and through the adoptive parents as if born to them, and that includes children a court treats as equitably adopted (Sec. 201.054). Birth parents and their kindred cannot inherit from or through an adopted child.

A child counts as a father's child for inheritance in specific cases: birth within a marriage as described in Family Code Sec. 160.201, a court decree, adoption, or a signed acknowledgment of paternity (Sec. 201.052). Someone claiming to be a biological child can petition the probate court, which must find it by clear and convincing evidence. The person must also have been born before the death or be in gestation then, and survive at least 120 hours (Sec. 201.056).

Half siblings take half as much as whole siblings when both inherit together, and a group made up only of half siblings each takes a whole share (Sec. 201.057). These rules can change who has to sign a deed, so an overlooked child is the biggest risk in a quick family sale.

Proving who the heirs are so the house can be sold

Texas offers several routes, and the right one depends on the estate. Each ends with a document the county clerk can record.

  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement filed with the county clerk. No court reviews it, and no law forces a title company or buyer to accept it.
  • Determination of heirship: a probate court hearing that ends in an order naming the heirs.
  • Small estate affidavit: available only when the estate is within the dollar limit in Estates Code ch. 205, assets are enough to pay debts, and the court approves. A house other than the homestead is a problem here, because the chapter excludes real property except a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children.
  • Administration: the court appoints an administrator, who can later sign a deed.

A buyer who pays value and relies in good faith on a recorded affidavit of heirship that omits a child can still get good title (Sec. 201.053), though the heirs remain liable to the omitted child for the sale proceeds. That rule protects the buyer, not the siblings who signed.

Selling an inherited house when there is no will

A typical sale follows a short chain of steps, and the order matters because each one supports the next.

  1. Get a certified death certificate and list every relative who could be an heir.
  2. Pick a route to establish title: affidavit, heirship hearing, small estate affidavit where it fits, or administration.
  3. Record the proof with the county clerk in the county where the house sits.
  4. Have every heir, or the court-appointed representative, sign the deed or contract.
  5. Settle the property tax bill. Texas property taxes attach as a lien each January 1, so an unpaid balance travels with the house.

An heir who wants the homestead exemption on the inherited home may be asked by the appraisal district for an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation, if the heir is not on a recorded deed.

Keeping the family on the same page

Intestate sales go smoothly when every heir knows the plan before a buyer appears. Hold one meeting, share the list of heirs and the route you picked, and agree in writing who will talk to the title company and who signs.

If one relative cannot be found or will not cooperate, tell the title company early. A court order may be the only route a buyer will accept in that case. A cash buyer can close quickly once title is cleared, but the proof of heirship still has to be recorded first.

Frequently asked questions

If my parent died without a will, do I own the house right away?

As an heir under Chapter 201, your interest passes at death, but the record title does not change by itself. You need a recorded affidavit, a court order or an administrator's deed before a buyer or title company treats the sale as clean.

Does a surviving spouse always get the house?

No. A spouse takes the whole community estate only when every child is also the spouse's child or there are no descendants. With separate property and children, the spouse gets a life estate in one third of the land and the children hold the remainder.

Can an affidavit of heirship be used to sell an inherited house?

Sometimes. It is a sworn statement filed with the county clerk, and no law makes a third party accept it. Many title companies ask for a court order instead when the family tree is unclear.

What if there is a child nobody listed?

The child can still claim a share. A buyer who relied in good faith on a recorded affidavit keeps good title under Sec. 201.053, but the heirs who sold must answer to that child for the proceeds.

Do siblings inherit if the owner had no spouse or children?

Yes, in the order the statute sets. If both parents are alive they take equal shares. If neither parent is alive, the siblings and their descendants take the whole estate.

In Texas a will does not prove title to property until it is admitted to probate (Estates Code Sec. 256.001), and it generally must be offered within four years of the testator's death. This guide covers what Chapter 256 says about the application, proof, the order and later challenges.

Probate and selling an inherited Texas house

Probate is the court procedure that turns a death into a clear owner on paper. A buyer's title company wants that paper before it insures anything, so a Texas house tied to an estate generally waits on one of several routes before it can change hands.

Texas has no single statewide probate office. Each filing lands in a particular county, so the practical work is local even though the rules come from state law. The county clerk's office can tell you what it will accept.

Think of the process as three questions. Was there a will? Does the estate owe anything beyond a mortgage? Do all the heirs agree? The answers point to the route in the table below.

How long an heir can wait to offer a will

The usual limit is four years after the person dies, and the court may take a later application for an acceptable reason.

A signed will sitting in a drawer gives nobody authority over the house. If a relative died several years ago and nobody opened an estate, count the years first. A probate attorney, or the clerk of the probate court in the county of the person's last home, can say what the file shows.

  • A formal will is in writing, signed, and witnessed by two people.
  • A will in the maker's own handwriting needs no witnesses.
  • The application normally goes to the probate court for the county of the person's last residence.

Which probate routes fit a house?

The route depends on whether a will exists, what the estate owes and whether the heirs agree.

Routes to clear title on an estate house
RouteTypical situationPaper a buyer will see
Full administrationWill exists and a representative must collect assets and pay debtsCourt order, then an executor's or administrator's deed
Muniment of titleWill exists, nothing owed except real estate liens, no administration neededCourt order plus the will, filed with the clerk for the land's county
Small estate affidavitNo will, $75,000 or less in assets excluding homestead and exempt propertyCourt-approved affidavit; the homestead copy is recorded
Heirship affidavitFamily swears to who the heirs areSworn statement filed with the clerk
Transfer on death deedOwner signed and recorded one while aliveRecorded affidavit of death and death certificate

No route is quick by default. The best one is whichever the estate actually qualifies for.

When a muniment of title makes sense

It suits a family with a valid will, no creditors beyond liens on real estate, and no need for a personal representative to run the estate. The judge admits the will and issues an order, and both documents are filed in the land records of the house's county.

For a seller this is often the tidiest result, because a title company can read the recorded order and see who took the house under the will. A surprise debt from a credit card or medical bill can push the estate into full administration, so ask the family attorney to confirm that nothing else is owed.

Who can use a small estate affidavit?

Only estates with no will and no administration underway, assets under the $75,000 line (homestead and exempt property left out), enough assets to cover the debts and agreement among every heir. Estates Code chapter 205 sets these terms.

Two limits catch families off guard. The estate cannot hold land other than a homestead that passes to a spouse or minor children, and the court must approve the affidavit. Two disinterested witnesses swear to it, 30 days must pass after the death and no petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted.

  • A second house or rental lot usually rules this route out.
  • One heir who objects stops it.
  • Ask the clerk which forms the local court expects.

Heirship statements and transfer on death deeds

Either can sometimes stand in for probate, with a catch for each. The heirship statement is sworn and filed with the clerk without any judge reviewing it, and nothing obliges a buyer, lender or title company to rely on it.

The transfer on death deed is different because the owner prepared it before dying. It moves land outside probate, can be revoked by the owner and has to reach the land records before the owner dies. Afterward the heirs record an affidavit of death with the death certificate. The related Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate, lets the owner sell or mortgage without asking the people named to inherit.

When neither exists, the court options are a determination of heirship or an order of no administration.

Who signs the deed to the buyer?

The signer follows the route. A court-appointed executor or administrator signs after full administration. After a muniment, the heirs named in the will take title and sign. After a transfer on death deed, the beneficiary who recorded the affidavit signs as owner.

The clerk cannot add names to an older deed, so the proof of how title moved has to sit in the land records before the sale closes. The deed itself needs a notary or similar officer to witness the signature. Ask the clerk for the current recording charges, which follow a per-page schedule with local add-ons.

Property tax and the homestead exemption after a death

Property tax keeps running. Each year's tax lien arises at the start of the year, and the person who owned the house then is the one liable.

Texas ended its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752, effective September 1, 2015. Heirs living in the house may keep claiming a homestead exemption. Heirs missing from a recorded deed hand the appraisal district a sworn ownership statement, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. A spouse who is 55 or older may in some cases carry over the over-65 exemption. The appraisal district has the current forms.

What heirs should gather before calling a buyer

Gather the paper that proves authority, then list what the sale must pay off. Missing authority is the most common reason an inherited sale stalls.

  • The will, if one exists, and the date of death.
  • The case number from the probate court, or confirmation that none is open.
  • A search of the land records for a transfer on death deed.
  • Mortgage and tax balances, since both are settled from the proceeds.
  • A decision among heirs about who signs.

In order, the work usually runs like this: confirm whether a will exists, pick the route, get the court order or affidavit, record it with the county clerk, clear the tax and mortgage balances, then sign the deed at closing.

A title company can say what it needs before closing, and an attorney can confirm which route fits the estate. Once the order, affidavit or deed is on record, the house can sell like any other, and a cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's appraisal or underwriting.

Frequently asked questions

What is the time limit to probate a will in Texas?

Four years after the death, as a general rule. A court can accept an application filed later when the applicant explains the delay acceptably.

Can heirs sell an estate house before the court finishes?

Usually not to a buyer who needs title insurance. The buyer will want an executor's deed, muniment order or approved affidavit on record first.

What is the asset ceiling for a Texas small estate affidavit?

$75,000, with the homestead and exempt items left out of the count. The estate must also have no will, no open administration and unanimous heirs.

Is there a Texas inheritance tax today?

No. Senate Bill 752 repealed it as of September 1, 2015, though property tax stays due.

Which office records probate documents for a house?

The county clerk for the county holding the house. The clerk records the deed or order once it carries a proper signature and notarization.

In Texas, neither spouse can sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other spouse's signature, whether the homestead is separate or community property. That rule is in Family Code Sec. 5.001. The code also sets who manages community and separate property and has a court process for selling when a spouse has disappeared or abandoned the home.

Spouse not on board, or missing?
Tell us about the situation. We buy as-is and work with a title company on what a sale needs.

Can one spouse sell the family home in Texas?

Not alone, if the house is the homestead. Family Code Sec. 5.001 provides that whether the homestead is one spouse's separate property or community property, neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber it without the other spouse joining, unless the chapter or other law provides an exception.

That rule trips up sellers who hold title in one name. A deed signed by the titled spouse alone may leave the buyer without clear title, and a title company will ask about marital status before it commits to insure. A house that is not the homestead, such as a rental the couple owns, follows the management rules in Chapter 3 instead.

Community property versus separate property

Chapter 3 of the Family Code sorts property by when and how it was acquired. The sorting controls who may sign and who shares in the proceeds.

  • Separate property: what a spouse owned or claimed before marriage, what a spouse received during marriage by gift, devise or descent, and personal injury recoveries other than lost earning capacity (Sec. 3.001).
  • Community property: everything else either spouse acquired during marriage (Sec. 3.002).
  • Presumption: property possessed by either spouse during or at the end of the marriage is presumed community, and proving it separate takes clear and convincing evidence (Sec. 3.003).

A house bought during the marriage with wages is community even when only one name is on the deed. A house one spouse inherited is separate, though the other spouse may still have homestead rights in it if the couple lives there.

Managing property that is not the homestead

Each spouse has sole management of their own separate property (Sec. 3.101). For community property, Sec. 3.102 gives each spouse sole control of the community property that spouse would have owned if single, such as personal earnings and revenue from separate property. Anything else is under joint management unless the spouses agree otherwise by written power of attorney or another agreement.

Section 3.104 protects outsiders. During marriage, property held in one spouse's name is presumed to be under that spouse's sole control, and a third person who deals with that spouse can rely on it if they are not part of a fraud and have no notice of a lack of authority. That presumption does not override the homestead rule, which is why an investor buying a homestead still needs both signatures.

When the other spouse is missing or cannot sign

The Family Code has two court tracks, and both start with a sworn petition. Subchapter B of Chapter 5 covers the homestead itself, and Subchapter D of Chapter 3 covers other community property.

Court options when a spouse cannot join the sale
SituationStatuteWhat the law provides
Spouse declared incapacitated by a guardianship courtSec. 5.002 and 5.003Competent spouse may sell without the other's joinder
Spouse disappeared, abandoned the home, or permanently separatedSec. 5.101 and 5.102Sworn petition to sell without joinder
Spouse reported prisoner of war or missing on public serviceSec. 5.101(4) and 5.102(4)Petition allowed, with a court-appointed attorney for the respondent
Community property other than the homesteadSec. 3.301Petition to manage and dispose of described community property

How the court process starts and what the judge can order

A petitioning spouse cannot file at once. Section 5.103 sets the earliest filing at the 60th day after the disappearance, abandonment or permanent separation, and at six months after a spouse is reported as a prisoner of war or missing on public service. The petition goes to a court in a county where any part of the property is located.

The judge may appoint an attorney for the respondent, and must do so when the respondent is reported as a prisoner of war or missing. If the spouse's residence is unknown, citation by publication runs for two consecutive weeks before the hearing under Sec. 3.305.

Under Sec. 5.106 and 3.306, the court may attach conditions to protect the other spouse, require a bond, and order some or all sale proceeds paid into the court registry. An order that affects real property is not constructive notice to a good faith purchaser unless it is recorded in the deed records of the county where the land sits (Sec. 3.308).

Plan your sale timeline around that waiting period. If a buyer is lined up, tell the title company about the petition early so it can say what order it will need to see at closing.

When a spouse dies

Estates Code ch. 201 governs a death without a will. The community estate passes to the surviving spouse when the decedent left no descendants, or when all surviving children are also the spouse's children. If a child from another relationship survives, the decedent's undivided one-half interest in the community passes to that child line, charged with community debts.

Separate property follows other rules. With children, the surviving spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the land. With no children, the spouse takes half of the land. A title policy generally does not cover homestead, community property or survivorship rights of a policyholder's spouse, so a clean spousal signature or court order matters to the buyer.

Written agreements that change ownership

Sec. 3.410 recognizes premarital and marital property agreements that meet Chapter 4 requirements, and such an agreement can waive, release, assign or partition reimbursement claims. Sec. 3.004 separately allows a signed and acknowledged schedule of a spouse's separate property to be recorded in the deed records.

The recording matters for real estate. A schedule of separate real property is not constructive notice to a good faith purchaser or an unaware creditor unless it is acknowledged and recorded in the deed records of the county where the land sits. Anyone relying on such an agreement to sell without a spouse should talk with a Texas family law attorney first, because the homestead rule in Sec. 5.001 still applies to the house the couple lives in.

Reimbursement claims and a sale

One marital estate can owe another when it paid for the other's debts or improvements. Under Sec. 3.404 a reimbursement claim does not create an ownership interest, but it is a claim against the benefited estate that matures on divorce or death. On divorce or death, a court may impose an equitable lien on the benefited property under Sec. 3.406.

This often arises when community wages paid down a mortgage on a house one spouse owned before marriage. Raise the point with your closing attorney before listing, since a lien claim can show up in a divorce decree and a recorded document.

Frequently asked questions

Do both spouses have to sign a deed to sell a Texas homestead?

Yes, in general. Family Code Sec. 5.001 provides that neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other spouse joining, whether it is separate or community property, except where the code provides otherwise.

What if my spouse left and I cannot find them?

Sec. 5.102 lets you file a sworn petition to sell a community homestead without joinder when the spouse has disappeared, permanently abandoned the home, or the spouses are permanently separated. You cannot file until the 60th day after the event.

Is a house I bought before marriage community property?

No, it is separate property under Sec. 3.001. If the couple makes it their homestead, the spouse's signature is still required for a sale under Sec. 5.001 unless an exception applies.

Can a spouse sell if the other has dementia?

If a guardianship court has declared the other spouse incapacitated, Sec. 5.002 and 5.003 let the competent spouse sell without joinder. Without that judicial declaration, a power of attorney or court order is the usual route.

Does a divorce decree change who can sell?

It can. A decree usually awards the house to one spouse and may order a sale. Title companies ask for a recorded decree or deed so the buyer can see who holds title, and a Sec. 3.406 lien may also appear.

What a deed of trust does

When a Texas buyer finances a home, the closing papers nearly always include a deed of trust. It pledges the house as collateral and typically hands the lender a power of sale, so a loan that goes bad can end at a public auction rather than in a courtroom.

Two documents travel together. The promissory note is your promise to repay. The deed of trust attaches the house to that promise. After the last payment, the lender signs a release of lien, and the clerk records it so anyone searching the records sees the debt is gone.

The state allows three foreclosure routes:

  • Judicial foreclosure, a full lawsuit, which is rare in Texas.
  • Nonjudicial foreclosure, which uses the sale power written into the deed of trust and is the everyday method under Property Code section 51.002.
  • Expedited foreclosure, which starts with a court order. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and some owners' association assessment liens must go this way.

How nonjudicial foreclosure works

Expect a string of written notices and then an auction. Nobody in a courtroom approves the sale, which makes the statutory deadlines the main safeguard a borrower has.

For most home loans, federal rules hold the servicer back until the account is more than 120 days delinquent. Then comes the notice of default. A borrower who pays everything past due within 20 days of receiving it reinstates the loan, as section 51.002(d) provides.

If nothing is paid, the servicer issues a notice of sale at least three weeks ahead of the auction. One copy goes on the courthouse door and another to the clerk. Open every letter the day it comes, since the printed dates are the ones that count.

Sale day and location

Foreclosure auctions are open to anyone and are held in daytime hours on the first Tuesday of each month. If that Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, the sale slides to the Wednesday.

Your notice prints the start time, and bidding has to open within three hours after it. Where in the county it happens is set by the commissioners court, and the clerk can point you to the designated spot.

Note versus deed of trust when you sell

For a seller the distinction shows up in paperwork. Request a payoff statement from the servicer, and let the title company make sure the lien is released when closing funds pay off the loan.

Suppose the loan is already in default. A buyer who pays it off ahead of the auction gets the house with the lien cleared from the record. Someone who wins at the auction receives a trustee's deed instead, recorded by the county clerk.

Because one office records everything, a title search lists each deed of trust, release and foreclosure notice in sequence. Walk through that chain to learn who has a lien on your home and whether a document is missing.

What happens after the sale?

The high bidder gets the house, but the debt may not be fully settled. When the bid is lower than what was owed, the lender has two years from the sale to bring a deficiency suit. The former owner can ask the judge to offset the home's fair market value.

A bid above the debt creates surplus money, which pays junior lienholders first and the former owner last. Do not count on buying the house back. Texas has no general redemption right after a deed of trust sale, only narrow ones such as certain tax liens and owners' association assessment liens.

An occupant who stays after the auction can force the new owner into an eviction case. The eviction pages on this site cover that court path.

Recording and releasing with the county clerk

Deed records live with the county clerk. Your deed of trust, its release and any trustee's deed after a sale all end up in that one record.

A real property instrument can be recorded when it carries a signature and an acknowledgment, or an oath taken before two subscribing witnesses or an authorized officer (Property Code section 12.001(b)). Standard fees in the 2023 clerk manual run like this:

  • $5.00 for page one, then $4.00 for each added page or attachment.
  • $0.25 for each name over five that has to be indexed.
  • A records management and preservation fee of no more than $10 and a records archive fee of no more than $10.
  • A records technology and infrastructure fee of $2.00.

These amounts change over time, so call the clerk for today's schedule. Once your loan is paid off, look in the clerk's index to confirm the release was recorded.

Checking a notice before you act

Look at the notice itself before anything else. Confirm the sale date falls on the first Tuesday or the Wednesday substitute, and that the county named is the one where the house sits. Check the date of the letter against the date you received it, because the 20-day cure period runs from receipt.

If something looks off, write to the servicer, keep a copy, and show the letter to an attorney quickly. The window to act ends at the auction.

If your loan is in default

Your best first step is to use the 20-day window. Ask the servicer what exact amount cures the default, and get the number in writing. If the window closes, options remain, but each one is now racing the sale date.

Owners in default commonly look at these choices:

  • Bring the loan current with a reinstatement payment.
  • Ask the servicer about a repayment plan or loan modification before the sale date.
  • Sell the house before the first Tuesday sale, so the proceeds pay the lender and any remaining equity stays with you.
  • Talk to a Texas attorney or a legal aid office about your specific notice.

Selling ahead of the auction usually leaves a tidier record than a foreclosure, since the lien gets paid and released instead of enforced. Before you talk to anyone, collect the default notice, the sale notice and your loan statements. Buyers and title companies ask for all three.

When time is short, a cash sale can close fast because it skips the buyer's lender underwriting and appraisal. Your own servicer still has to be paid off at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

Does Texas require a court order to foreclose on a deed of trust?

Usually not. Nonjudicial foreclosure under the power of sale needs no court order. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and certain owners' association assessment liens need an expedited court order instead.

How long is the cure period after a notice of default?

Twenty days from receipt. Paying the overdue amount in that span reinstates the loan under Property Code section 51.002(d). Ask the servicer for a written reinstatement figure so the amount is exact.

Can a Texas foreclosure sale happen on any day?

No. Sales are set for the first Tuesday of the month, or the first Wednesday when January 1 or July 4 falls on that Tuesday. The notice gives a start time, and bidding must begin within three hours of it.

Can I still owe money after the house is sold at auction?

Possibly. A deficiency suit is allowed for two years after the sale, and you may ask for a credit based on the home's fair market value. Surplus sale money goes to junior liens first and then to you.

Where do I find recorded deeds of trust and releases?

Search the clerk's records in the county where the property sits. The clerk records deeds of trust, releases, trustee's deeds and foreclosure sale notices, and charges the filing fees set by statute.

How foreclosure works in Texas

On most Texas homes, a foreclosure is a courthouse auction run by the lender after a sequence of notices, without a lawsuit. This is nonjudicial foreclosure, and it rests on the power of sale in the deed of trust.

Judicial foreclosure exists but is uncommon. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and owners' association assessment liens must go through an expedited court order instead. Your loan papers tell you which route applies.

When a lender can start

On most home loans, federal rules prevent the servicer from beginning foreclosure until you are more than 120 days behind. That leaves a stretch of time to talk with the servicer before any formal notice shows up.

Texas also puts a clock on the lender. Civil Practice and Remedies Code section 16.035 sets a four-year limitations period for foreclosure actions, with exceptions. If you are holding an old default notice, ask an attorney whether that period matters.

Notices you will receive

Two notices drive the process, and each one starts a deadline.

  • Notice of default: you can reinstate by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving it (Property Code section 51.002(d)).
  • Notice of sale: sent after the 20 days pass, with 21 days or more before the auction.
  • Posting and filing: the notice of sale goes on the courthouse door and to the county clerk, who charges $2.00 per notice under the 2023 clerk manual.
  • Military statement: the notice has to include the active-duty military statement.

Save every letter and write down the postmark.

Sale date and location

Sales are held on the first Tuesday of the month, shifting to the Wednesday when that Tuesday is New Year's Day or Independence Day. The window runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and bidding starts at the time in the notice or within three hours after it.

The auction takes place at a location inside the property's own county. The commissioners court chooses it and records it in the real property records.

Where the money and the debt go

The bid pays the foreclosing lender first. Anything left over goes to junior lienholders and then to the former owner.

If the bid falls short, the lender can sue for the difference, but a deficiency suit has to be filed within two years of the sale. You can ask the court for a fair market value offset. After a property tax foreclosure sale, the former owner has two years from the sale to claim excess proceeds.

Can you redeem the house after foreclosure?

Generally no, not after a deed of trust sale. Redemption rights apply to narrow situations such as certain tax liens and owners' association assessment liens.

For a tax sale, the Texas Supreme Court has described Tax Code section 34.21 as follows. Homestead, agricultural and mineral interest property can be redeemed for two years after the purchaser's deed is filed, with a premium of 25 percent in the first year or 50 percent in the second. Other property can be redeemed by the 180th day after filing, with a premium of no more than 25 percent. The owner also repays the purchaser's bid and the added charges the opinion lists.

Ways to avoid foreclosure

Write to the servicer early so you have a paper trail. Each option below races the auction date.

  • Reinstate within the 20-day cure period.
  • Request a repayment plan or modification from the servicer.
  • Sell the home before the first Tuesday sale.

A sale ahead of the auction pays off the lien and keeps a trustee's deed out of the county records. Collect your default notice, sale notice and loan statements before you speak with a buyer. A cash buyer can often close fast because there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on.

Foreclosure paperwork at the county level

Texas has 254 counties, and each county clerk keeps its own foreclosure record. The clerk records deeds of trust, liens and notices of foreclosure sale, and also serves as clerk of the commissioners court.

That second job helps you, because the commissioners court designates where sales happen. If you cannot tell where an auction will take place, ask the clerk. Rural and urban offices apply the same law but differ in hours and in how notices can be searched.

  • Contact the clerk where the house is located, not where you live.
  • Ask for the current list of posted notices of sale.
  • Ask where the commissioners court designated the sale area.
  • Ask how filings are accepted and what the fee will be.

Documents to gather

Put everything about the loan in one folder before you speak with a servicer, an attorney or a buyer. With the dates in front of you, the nearest deadline is easy to spot.

  • The note and deed of trust from closing.
  • The notice of default and its envelope or delivery record.
  • The notice of sale and the date printed on it.
  • Recent loan statements and any servicer letters.
  • Proof of homestead use if you live in the house.

If property taxes are behind, remember that each year's tax lien arises on the first of January and a lender may pay the taxes and add them to your balance. Ask your servicer how taxes are being handled.

Why the dates on your notices matter

Each protection a Texas borrower has hangs on a date printed on a piece of paper. The cure period starts when the default letter arrives, and the auction cannot be held until the sale letter has aged enough. Mark each date on a calendar the day the mail comes.

If something looks wrong, such as a sale date that is not a Tuesday or a county other than the one where the house sits, tell the servicer in writing and see an attorney quickly. Small errors in timing or place can matter, and your window closes at the auction.

Keep a simple log: the date each letter was received, who sent it, and what it demanded. If you later sell or negotiate with the servicer, that log answers most of the questions anyone will ask.

If someone is still in the house after the sale

An auction buyer who finds an occupant may need an eviction case to get possession. The notice and justice court steps are on this site's eviction pages.

Allow for that gap. The buyer holds title at the auction but not automatic possession, and a seller who stays past the sale can expect a notice to vacate.

Frequently asked questions

Is foreclosure in Texas judicial or nonjudicial?

Mostly nonjudicial, using the power of sale in the deed of trust. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and some association liens need an expedited court order.

What is the reinstatement deadline on a Texas loan?

Twenty days from receipt of the default notice. Pay the past-due balance in that period, as section 51.002(d) of the Property Code provides.

How much notice comes before a Texas foreclosure sale?

At least 21 days. The notice must be posted on the courthouse door and filed with the clerk.

Can the lender still sue me after the auction?

Yes, for a shortfall, if it files a deficiency suit within two years of the sale. You may request a fair market value offset.

What day are Texas foreclosure auctions held?

The first Tuesday of each month. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the first Wednesday is used instead.

Who pays which Texas closing costs depends mostly on the contract. The Texas Real Estate Commission's resale contract, Form 20-19, splits them: the seller pays lien releases, tax certificates, deed preparation and half the escrow fee, and the buyer pays loan costs and the other half of the escrow fee. This guide summarizes that form and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's description of closing costs.

Who pays closing costs when a Texas house sells?

The sales contract decides, and in most resale deals the contract is the standard One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, with an effective date of July 1, 2026. It is the most frequently used contract for single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes.

The form does not cover condominiums, new homes sold by a builder, or farm and ranch property. Those use other forms, so a seller of one of those property types should check which contract applies before negotiating. Ask your agent or title company to walk you through the cost paragraphs of whichever form is used, since individual lines can be changed by negotiation.

What a seller typically sees on the closing statement

Expect charges tied to clearing title and settling the year's taxes, plus anything you agreed to cover in the contract.

  • Payoff of any mortgage or other lien, so the lienholder's claim is released at funding.
  • Property taxes for your share of the year, because the lien attaches on January 1 and the buyer cannot get clear title with delinquent taxes outstanding.
  • The owner's title policy premium, if the contract assigns it to you.
  • Escrow, tax certificate and delivery charges, which many title companies add.
  • Recording charges for any release or curative document you must file.
  • Seller concessions, if you agreed to contribute toward the buyer's costs.

Lenders must give buyers a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing. A seller can ask the title company for a draft settlement statement in the same window.

The owner's title policy

The buyer and seller may negotiate who pays for it. The premium is paid once at closing, and the parties can agree on who bears it.

The amount itself is not negotiable with the title company. Texas title rates are regulated, and every title company charges the same premium for a given policy. The basic premium is $496 for a $50,000 property and $832 for a $100,000 property. That premium covers the title search, examination and closing service, so you are not billed separately for those pieces.

Title insurance is not required by Texas law, though a lender will require a loan policy. You may pick any title company, and RESPA bars a seller from conditioning the sale on a particular insurer.

Before closing day

Gather the paperwork and questions early, because a Texas closing moves quickly once a contract is signed.

  • Get a payoff letter from each lender with a lien on the property.
  • Ask the escrow officer for a draft settlement statement as soon as one exists.
  • Confirm in writing who pays the owner's policy premium and which escrow fees fall to you.
  • Pull the current tax bill and note the year's due dates.
  • If the property is held by a married couple, confirm both spouses will sign.

Those steps cost nothing and tend to catch errors while there is still time to fix them. On the day itself, bring a government photo ID and the keys, garage openers and any warranty papers the contract says you will hand over. A cash sale usually skips the lender's extra conditions, so the list of things that can hold up funding is shorter.

Title commitment versus title policy

The commitment arrives before closing and the policy is issued afterward. The commitment says the company is willing to insure the buyer on stated conditions, including any problems the seller must fix. It lists potential issues, exclusions and exceptions, and it does not promise that no problem exists.

For a seller, the commitment is the early warning. It can reveal a lien, an unpaid judgment or a gap in the chain of ownership while there is still time to cure it. Common title defects include forged or improperly witnessed documents, unrecorded easements, liens for unpaid taxes or association charges, and claims from missing heirs.

Read the commitment as soon as the buyer's title company produces it, and ask the escrow officer which items you are expected to clear. A seller who clears them quickly avoids a delayed funding date.

Other charges a title company can add

Escrow fees differ between companies, and tax certificates, escrow, recording and delivery are common add-ons beyond the premium. You may review the closing papers ahead of time and bring a lawyer.

A missing grantee mailing address may add $25. Counties may differ on capped charges, so confirm the current schedule with your clerk.

Property taxes and the sale

Bills go out around October 1, and delinquency begins February 1 for most. Penalty and interest accrue from there.

Because that year's lien attaches on January 1, a closing early in the year can find the prior bill still open. Whoever owned on that January date remains liable, even after selling. So request the tax certificate at the start of the process and make sure the payoff covers any unpaid year.

Buyers who take title after January 1 may be able to claim the school homestead exemption for the rest of that year if the seller never held it. Mention that to your buyer.

Is there a transfer tax on the deed?

The charge on a deed is the recording fee shown above. A county clerk records instruments for the county in which the land lies, and the instrument has to be acknowledged or sworn before an authorized officer.

A draft settlement statement shows every government charge before you commit. If a line looks unfamiliar, ask the escrow officer what it pays for and who receives it. Corrections are easiest before the day of signing, when the figures are still a draft. Keep a copy of the corrected statement for your records.

Closing costs and your federal tax result

They can change it. Gain is measured from your adjusted basis and amount realized, and the federal home-sale exclusion applies to what remains. Publication 523 explains which selling expenses count. Texas imposes no state income tax, so the question is federal only.

Who pays closing costs when selling a house in Texas?

It depends on the contract. The resale form 20-19 is the most frequently used, and each cost line can be negotiated. Read the cost paragraphs with your agent or title company before signing.

Can I negotiate the title insurance premium in Texas?

No. The premium is regulated and every title company charges the same amount for a policy. What you can negotiate with the buyer is who pays it, and you can compare escrow and other fees between companies.

Is title insurance required to sell a Texas home?

Texas does not require it. A buyer's lender will require a loan policy, and buyers often purchase an owner's policy as well. The contract says who pays for it.

What are the recording fees for a Texas deed?

The county clerk manual prints $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for later pages, plus capped records fees. Counties differ on some charges, so get today's schedule from the clerk.

Will I owe property tax at closing if I sell in the spring?

Possibly. The lien attaches each January 1 and most bills are delinquent after January 31, so the prior year must be paid and the current year divided between you and the buyer. The settlement statement shows the split.

Skip the Contract Hassle: Get a Cash Offer for Your Texas House

The Texas Real Estate Commission's One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026, leaves the option period length as a blank for the parties to fill in. During that period the buyer can terminate for any reason by giving notice by 5:00 p.m. local time. This guide walks through the option period, the Seller's Disclosure Notice, title deadlines and default remedies as the form states them.

Prefer a simple as-is sale?
No inspection negotiations, no repair requests and no agent commission. Get a written cash offer.

What the option period is

The option period is a window in which a buyer who paid an agreed option fee can end the contract for any reason by giving the seller written notice. The termination option is a negotiable term, so a buyer does not have to pay for one.

Buyers typically use the days to inspect the house and negotiate repairs through an amendment, or to walk away. For a seller, the period is the stretch in which the deal can end without the buyer giving a reason, so the numbers written into the contract matter.

Which contract form applies in 2026?

Resale of a single family home, duplex, triplex or fourplex uses the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, with an effective date of July 1, 2026. It is the most frequently used contract form.

It is not for condominium sales, new homes sold by a builder, or farm and ranch property, and TREC publishes separate forms for those. TREC's contracts page also offers many addenda, including a third party financing addendum, a seller financing addendum, a short sale addendum and a back-up contract addendum.

Option fee and earnest money

The buyer delivers earnest money and the option fee to the escrow agent. An earlier edition of the form, in paragraph 5A, required delivery within three days of the effective date. Paragraph 5D set the consequence: if no option fee amount is stated or the buyer fails to deliver it on time, the buyer has no unrestricted right to terminate under that paragraph.

Paragraph numbers and day counts can shift between editions, so read the current 20-19 itself or ask your agent or title company to point them out. Days count from the effective date, with the first day being the next day, and each day is a calendar day.

  • Option fee: set by the parties, paid to the seller for the termination right.
  • Earnest money: held by the escrow agent.
  • Option days: a negotiated number written into the contract.
  • Notice: written, delivered to the other side.

How days are counted

The count starts with the effective date, which is the date of final signature, and the first day of any period is the day after. Every day is a calendar day, so weekends and holidays count. If you sign on a Friday, Saturday is day one. Ask your agent to mark the end date on a calendar.

Send deadline notices the way the contract's notice paragraph requires, because a missed deadline can change what a party may do. TREC does not decide whether a contract is valid or which party wins a dispute, so keep a dated copy of every notice sent or received.

When the buyer never pays earnest money

TREC's forms require the buyer to deliver earnest money to the escrow agent. If the buyer does not deliver it on time, the seller may terminate or exercise remedies under the contract's default paragraph. TREC has no jurisdiction to decide who is entitled to earnest money.

If a dispute over earnest money arises, talk to a private attorney. TREC has no authority over title companies, though it can take complaints about a license holder who fails to deposit earnest money as the contract requires.

What a Texas seller must disclose

Give the notice completely and accurately, and ask your agent how to answer any question about repairs or known defects. A mistake in completing a form can lead to financial loss or an unenforceable contract.

How repair terms and the option period fit together

A buyer should check the box for specific repairs only if particular repairs are known when the contract is signed. Otherwise the buyer checks the as-is box, and most buyers then pay for an option period to inspect and negotiate.

Repair paths in the resale contract
SituationWhat to do
Specific repairs known at signingUse the specific-repairs choice and list them
No known repairsUse the as-is choice
Repairs found by inspectionAmend the contract, or terminate during the option period
Boxes left blank or vagueNot permitted

As a seller, expect repair requests to come through an amendment after the buyer inspects. The option period is when that bargaining happens.

Can I use a TREC form without an agent?

Yes. The contract forms are available for public use, but they are intended primarily for brokers and sales agents trained in using them. A mistake in using a form may lead to financial loss or an unenforceable contract, and a person using a form accepts all risks that come with it.

A license holder who fills in a form may add only factual matters and business details to a form adopted for mandatory use. If TREC has not promulgated a form that you need, have an attorney draft it. A license holder may not draft an instrument that transfers or affects an interest in real property.

  • A Texas real estate attorney can draft terms the forms do not cover.
  • Members of the Texas Association of Realtors can use that group's forms.
  • Your title company can explain how it handles earnest money and the option fee.

What to check in the contract before you sign

Find the option days, the option fee, the earnest money amount and the repair choice. These are blanks or checkboxes that the parties fill in, and complete and accurate completion is the license holder's duty.

  • The effective date is filled in.
  • The option fee amount is stated, and a due date for delivery.
  • The earnest money amount and the escrow agent are named.
  • The repair paragraph has one choice marked, not both and not neither.
  • Any addendum, such as financing or a back-up contract, is attached.

Whether a contract with a blank effective date is valid is a question for a private attorney, so catch blanks before signing.

Ending the contract

A buyer who wants to terminate can use TREC's Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract form, and a seller has a matching Notice of Seller's Termination form. Notices need to reach the other side in the way the contract requires, so check the notice paragraph in your form.

License holders must use adopted contract forms and may add only factual matters and business details. No TREC form is meant to be a contract for deed. Anyone who needs something the forms do not cover should have an attorney prepare it. A blank effective date or a disputed term goes to a private attorney.

A seller weighing a cash buyer should know that option periods, financing addenda and repair amendments are all negotiable, and a cash offer often shortens or drops several of them. Read whatever terms a buyer proposes the same way you would read any other contract.

Frequently asked questions

Is an option period required in a Texas home contract?

No. The termination option is a negotiable term and a buyer does not have to pay for one. A buyer who pays the agreed fee gets the right to terminate for any reason by written notice during the option period.

How long is the option period?

The parties negotiate it, and the number of days is written into the contract. Check the figure in your signed form.

What if the buyer did not pay the option fee?

Probably no unrestricted termination right. A buyer who states no fee or fails to deliver it on time loses that right under the option paragraph.

Which form applies to my Texas house sale?

Form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026, for single family homes and two to four unit residential properties. TREC lists separate forms for condos, new builds and farm and ranch property.

Can TREC decide an earnest money dispute?

No. TREC lacks jurisdiction over who is entitled to earnest money and refers parties to a private attorney.

A Texas owner selling a home without an agent still has to give the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, and if the house will still be encumbered by a recorded lien at closing the seller must give a separate lien disclosure at least seven days before. Those duties are in Property Code Secs. 5.008 and 5.016.

Paperwork for a Texas sale without an agent

A Texas owner selling without an agent still has to hand the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, use a written contract, and record a signed and acknowledged deed with the county clerk. No agent is needed for any of those steps, but each one has rules attached.

The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) publishes the disclosure as Form 55-1 for sellers of previously occupied single family homes, and it applies to contracts entered into on or after September 1, 2023. It covers the material facts and physical condition of the property that Section 5.008 of the Property Code calls for.

  • Seller's Disclosure Notice (TREC 55-1) for a previously occupied single-family home
  • A federal lead-based paint disclosure if the house was built before 1978
  • A groundwater and surface water rights disclosure when the contract calls for it
  • Notice to Prospective Buyer (TREC 58-0), which covers title advice and utility district notices
  • A deed that is signed and acknowledged, then recorded in the land's home county

The TREC form page carries the current version. The Property Code lists situations where the notice is not required, so ask a Texas real estate attorney if you are unsure whether your sale qualifies.

Which disclosures apply?

Some disclosures come from state law, some from the standard TREC contract, and one from federal law. Which ones you need depends on the house and the contract.

Common disclosures for a Texas for-sale-by-owner house
DisclosureWhen it appliesPublished by
Seller's Disclosure Notice, Form 55-1Previously occupied single family residence, under Property Code Sec. 5.008TREC
Seller's Disclosure About Groundwater and Surface Water RightsDefault under TREC contracts unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) is trueTREC
Notice to Prospective Buyer, Form 58-0Abstract or title policy advice, and utility district noticesTREC
Lead-based paint disclosure and pamphletMost housing built before 1978U.S. EPA

Sellers are most often caught off guard by the water form. Nothing in state law demands it. It arrives with the TREC contract itself, and being exempt from the Seller's Disclosure Notice does not automatically release you from it. A well, pond, lake or water tank on the lot, or any known severed or leased groundwater right, can make the form necessary.

A surface water right is a permit, certified filing or certificate of adjudication issued by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for diverting, impounding or using surface water. Not sure whether your tract holds one? An attorney can tell you.

Federal rules for a house built before 1978

Older Texas houses bring a federal duty. The EPA's Lead-based Paint Disclosure Rule reaches most private housing from before 1978, and the seller carries it with or without an agent. It skips foreclosure sales, zero-bedroom units, newer construction, and homes a certified inspector has cleared of lead-based paint.

  • Hand over the EPA pamphlet, Protect Your Family From Lead In Your Home.
  • Tell the buyer everything you know about lead paint or lead hazards in the house, and pass along any reports you hold.
  • Put a Lead Warning Statement in the contract or attach it, with a line confirming you complied.
  • Give the buyer a 10-day window for a paint inspection or risk assessment. The buyer can waive it, or both sides can agree in writing to a different period.
  • File the signed disclosure for three years after closing.

Sample forms exist in English and Spanish on the EPA's site. A seller who ignores the rule can face penalties, so deal with it before you accept an offer.

Do I need a license to sell my own house in Texas?

A license is not required for an individual employed by a property owner to buy or sell real property on the owner's behalf (Rule 535.5(c)). For a sale of your own house, call TREC to confirm before relying on that answer.

The point matters most when title sits in an LLC or corporation and a family member or employee is handling the sale. It does not cover selling a property you do not own or taking a fee to market someone else's house. If the facts are unclear, a short call to a Texas real estate attorney costs less than a licensing complaint.

Recording the deed and clearing title

Take the finished deed to the clerk in the county where the land sits. A notary or another authorized officer must acknowledge the signature, or two subscribing witnesses must sign. The clerk accepts general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's and sheriff's deeds.

Recording fees are set locally. Dallas, Denton and Ellis counties each print a $25 first-page charge and $4 for later pages, with differences in add-ons. Ask the county clerk for the current fee page and any rules on return addresses, ID and payment, since those vary by county.

  • Title search. A title company or lawyer checks recorded liens, judgments and the chain of owners before closing.
  • Payoff and release. The payoff goes to the lender at closing, and the lender then records a release of lien.
  • Inherited houses. Banks and title companies are not bound to accept an affidavit of heirship, so you may need a muniment of title, executor's deed or transfer on death deed.
  • Contracts for deed. Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D covers executory contracts for residential property, and the purchaser has a statutory right to cancel.

Property taxes and exemptions in the year of sale

Whoever owns the house on January 1 is liable for that year's tax, because the lien attaches that day. Your contract should divide the year of sale between you and the buyer. Values are set as of January 1, bills arrive near October 1, and anything unpaid goes delinquent on February 1, drawing a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

If you never claimed a homestead exemption, a buyer who closes after January 1 can claim it for the rest of that year. School districts must grant a $140,000 residence homestead exemption, with an additional $60,000 school exemption for owners 65 or older or disabled. Carry your tax receipts, exemption letters and any over-65 ceiling paperwork to the title company so it can prorate properly.

Texas also caps annual increases in appraised value for a residence homestead at 10 percent.

Selling to stop a foreclosure

Non-judicial foreclosure in Texas moves on a tight schedule, and a sale before the auction can end it. Once a notice of default arrives, the borrower has 20 days to cure by paying what is past due. Next, the servicer must send a Notice of Sale at least 21 days ahead of the auction.

Sales are public and take place on the first Tuesday of the month between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the sale moves to the Wednesday. Call your servicer, read the sale date on the posted notice, and ask a title company to confirm the payoff before listing at a price buyers will actually pay.

What to gather before you list

Sales run smoother when your papers are ready the first time a buyer asks.

  • Your vesting deed, for the exact legal description and owner names.
  • A payoff letter from any lender with a lien.
  • The latest tax bill and exemption letters.
  • Repair and permit records, which help you complete the disclosure notice truthfully.
  • Details on any well, pond or water tank on the lot.

Armed with those, you can complete the Seller's Disclosure Notice and open a title order. Closing then follows a set pattern: you sign before a notary, your lender gets paid off, and the clerk records the deed.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to give a buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice if I sell my Texas house myself?

Usually, yes. Property Code Sec. 5.008 makes Form 55-1 the seller's job for a previously occupied single family residence, agent or not. A few situations in the statute are exempt.

Is the groundwater and surface water disclosure required by Texas law?

No other law requires it. It becomes part of the deal when the parties use a TREC contract, unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) of the One to Four Family Residential Contract is true.

What is TREC Form 58-0?

The Notice to Prospective Buyer. By signing, the buyer confirms being told to have an attorney examine the abstract or to buy title insurance. It also carries statutory notices for homes inside a utility district.

Does a federal lead paint disclosure apply to my Texas home?

Only if the house was built before 1978. For most private housing from that era, the EPA rule requires the pamphlet, a disclosure of what you know, a Lead Warning Statement and a 10-day inspection window for the buyer.

Where do I record the deed after a for-sale-by-owner closing in Texas?

With the clerk of the county where the house stands. Have the deed acknowledged by a notary or other authorized officer, or sign it before two subscribing witnesses. Fees and filing rules vary by county.
