content:
Texas Property Tax Guide: Rates, Due Dates, Penalties and Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Texas Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Texas Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Texas Property Taxes? Get a Cash Offer Before the Next Deadline

Unpaid property taxes can be paid from your sale proceeds at closing. Tell us about the house and get a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has no state property tax. Local taxing units set rates, appraisal districts set values, and taxes are due by January 31 of the year after the tax year. Taxes for 2026 are due by January 31, 2027, which is a Sunday, so under Tax Code Sec. 1.06 the last day without penalty is Monday, February 1, 2027. This guide covers the vocabulary, the penalty schedule and what happens if taxes go unpaid. For county and city details, use our Texas county property tax guides.

Behind on property taxes?
Get My Cash Offer →

Who sends the bill

Texas has no state property tax. What you owe is the sum of separate levies from the county, your school district, usually a city, and sometimes a hospital, junior college or other special district, all applied to the same house.

Value comes from the local appraisal district, whose chief appraiser looks at every parcel as it stood on January 1 and also processes exemption requests. A review board settles disputes. In many places the county tax assessor-collector sends a single combined statement each October on behalf of all the units.

The Texas tax calendar

Here are the ten dates a homeowner should know.

Texas property tax dates for a homeowner
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Value, exemption status and the year's tax lien are fixed
Apr. 1 or soon afterValue notices go out for single-family homesteads
Apr. 30Deadline for many exemption applications
May 1 or soon afterValue notices for other property
May 15Protest deadline, unless 30 days after the notice is later
July 25Chief appraiser certifies the roll
Sept. 29Most units adopt rates by this date, or within 60 days of the roll if later
Oct. 1Bills mailed
Nov. 30 and June 30Halves of a split payment
Jan. 31Final day without delinquency

Your bill arrives in October. January is the last month to pay without penalty.

How rates get set

Once the certified roll arrives, most units figure two benchmarks before voting. The no-new-revenue rate would raise the same money as last year from the same properties. The voter-approval rate is a ceiling, and a unit that wants to exceed it must go to the voters at the next uniform election date.

Each unit posts both rates on its homepage, announces the vote date in its notice, and, unless it is very small, holds a public hearing. You cannot argue a rate at your own protest hearing, only your value.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Late payment: penalties, waivers, plans

Money still owed when January closes goes past due on February 1. Six percent penalty and one percent interest land that very day. From then on the penalty creeps up a point every month until it tops out at twelve percent in July. Interest never stops and has no ceiling.

A unit that has retained a collection lawyer may add up to a fifth on top. Statute gives you 21 days to pay a bill, so a statement mailed after January 10 pushes the due date back. One dated January 15 is not past due until March 1.

Older or disabled owners may pay in four installments. The first falls due by February 1, then March 31, May 31 and July 31. Miss one and you owe six percent of it plus a monthly one percent.

  • You can ask in writing, before day 181, for the penalty and interest to be forgiven, provided you paid within 21 days of finding out you were behind.
  • Plans stretching up to 36 months exist at some offices, and a residence homestead is entitled to one.
  • Owners past 65 or disabled may split even a current bill four ways.

Homestead and other exemptions

Your homestead exemption is the largest discount available. A school district must knock $140,000 off the taxable value. Any other unit can choose a percentage cut instead, up to 20 percent, with a floor of $5,000.

  • Being 65 or older, or qualifying as disabled, adds $60,000 more off the school bill.
  • A service-connected disability rating takes between $5,000 and $12,000 off, and a house owned by someone rated 100 percent pays nothing.
  • A widow or widower aged 55 or more may inherit the late spouse's over-65 benefit in some cases.

File by the end of April. Bought after January 1 from an owner who never applied? You can still apply for that year.

What happens if taxes are never paid

Expect delinquent notices first, then perhaps a payment plan, then a lawsuit with court costs piled onto the balance. The suit can end with an auction conducted by a constable or a contracted agent. Sales are announced locally, so watch the county clerk and tax office websites.

Rights after the sale depend on what kind of property it was. Homestead, agricultural and mineral land can be redeemed within two years, and the former owner also has two years to claim excess sale proceeds. If you inherit a house with unpaid years on it, call the tax office quickly, because a payment plan may still be available.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Timing a sale around the tax year

January 1 fixes the lien, October 1 brings the bill and February 1 starts penalties. So a house that changes hands in spring is billed months later, and the closing agent splits the year between the two parties on the settlement statement. Listing in winter lets you clear the prior year before it turns past due.

Spring is also when appraisal notices land. If one arrives while you are under contract, tell your agent. A lower value after a protest changes the amount being split.

Limits on how fast a homestead bill can grow

Two guardrails protect homeowners. Once the exemption has been active a year, appraised value cannot jump more than 10 percent annually, new improvements aside.

Owners past 65 or disabled also receive a school tax ceiling locked in at the qualifying year, and a share of it can travel with them to another Texas residence. Counties, cities and junior college districts can adopt ceilings too, so ask each whether it did.

If the appraisal looks too high

Your first stop is the appraisal review board. The cutoff is May 15 or a month after the notice, whichever lands later. Unhappy with the outcome? Choose district court, regular binding arbitration, or, once the board's value tops $1,000,000, the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

Whichever path you pick, pay at least the part you do not dispute before the due date. Our protest guide covers the hearing step by step.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the tax office

Carry the account number, the address and the name on the deed. Ask for this year's amount, every earlier unpaid year, accrued penalty and interest, and any plan or waiver attached to the account. Request it in writing so everyone at closing works from the same numbers.

Inheriting? Find out which exemptions are active. An heir living there may need to refile personally.

Selling a house with taxes owed

The lien rides with the property, so no insurer will cover a buyer until earlier years are settled. Whoever owned on January 1 answers for that year even after selling and can be sued for it.

At closing the escrow officer pays old amounts out of your sale money and divides the current year. Get a tax certificate from the assessor-collector listing every unit, then check it against the settlement statement.

  • Look for past-due years, penalties and attorney fees.
  • Ask whether a payment plan is running.
  • The new owner applies for the homestead exemption afterward.

If back taxes, repairs and showings sound exhausting, a cash sale is another option. The balance gets paid from the proceeds at closing either way.

Frequently asked questions

Does Texas collect a state property tax?

No, the state collects none. Counties, cities, schools and special districts set their own rates and keep the money.

When is Texas property tax due?

Statements mail in October and are payable on receipt. Whatever remains after January 31 is past due on February 1. A split-payment arrangement, where offered, uses November 30 and June 30.

How much is the late charge?

Day one brings a six percent penalty and one percent interest. The penalty rises a point each month, reaching twelve percent in July.

How big is the homestead exemption?

A school district exempts $140,000, and owners who are older or disabled get $60,000 more. Other units may offer their own exemptions.

Can back taxes come out of a sale?

Yes. The closing agent typically pays them from the sale money, since the lien stays attached to the house.

Texas Homestead Exemption: Amounts, Over-65 Rules and Appraisal Cap

Cash Home Buyers in Texas

What the homestead exemption does

The exemption takes part of your home's appraised value out of the amount that local taxing units can tax, so your bill drops even though market value stays put. Appraisal districts value property as of January 1, so your status on that date drives the year's bill. There are three layers: a mandatory school district exemption, optional local exemptions, and extra relief for older or disabled owners.

Texas has no state property tax. Each taxing unit applies the exemption to its own levy, which means two neighbors served by different units can save different amounts.

General residence homestead exemption

Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) gives every residence homestead a $140,000 school district exemption. Under Sec. 11.13(n), any other taxing unit may choose a percentage exemption of up to 20 percent of value, with a $5,000 minimum.

  • School districts: $140,000, mandatory.
  • Cities, counties and others: optional, at the unit's discretion.
  • Counties with farm-to-market or flood control levies: $3,000 (Sec. 11.13(a)).

Each unit decides whether to offer a local option, so ask your appraisal district which of the units serving your address have done so.

Who qualifies as a homestead owner?

Two tests apply. You must own an interest in the house, and it must be where you mainly live. Claiming a second homestead, in Texas or anywhere else, disqualifies you.

If you buy mid-year, you can still get the exemption for the remaining months as long as the seller was not already receiving it. An heir who is not named on the recorded deed shows the appraisal district an ownership affidavit, the prior owner's death certificate, a utility bill and any court record citation.

Extra relief at age 65 or with a disability

An owner who is 65 or older, or disabled, gets another $60,000 at the school district level (Sec. 11.13(c)). Local units may add their own under Sec. 11.13(d), starting at $3,000.

Disability is judged by the Social Security benefit definition. In some cases a widow or widower aged 55 or more keeps the late spouse's over-65 benefit.

These owners also get a freeze on school tax. Under Sec. 11.26 the district cannot raise their total yearly bill on the homestead, with the first qualifying year's tax as the base. The freeze can follow the owner to a new Texas homestead, in proportion, and can continue for a surviving spouse aged 55 or older. Added improvements beyond ordinary repairs can lift it. Sec. 11.261 lets counties, cities and junior college districts adopt their own.

The 10 percent appraisal cap

After you qualify, the appraised value of your homestead can rise no more than 10 percent a year, apart from new improvements. Sec. 23.23 uses the lesser of market value or last year's appraised value plus 10 percent plus improvements.

The cap begins on the January 1 after your first qualifying year. It limits value only, so a higher rate from a taxing unit can still raise the bill.

Exemptions for disabled veteran owners

A disabled veteran gets an exemption on one property, scaled to the VA disability rating. Sec. 11.22 sets these amounts.

Sec. 11.22 exemption by VA disability rating
VA disability ratingExemption up to
10% to 29%$5,000
30% to 49%$7,500

70% to 100%$12,000

An owner aged 65 or older with a rating of at least 10 percent, one who is totally blind in one or both eyes, or one who lost use of a limb may receive $12,000. An unmarried surviving spouse and children under 18 may qualify too.

At a 100 percent rating, or 100 percent unemployability, the whole residence homestead is exempt under Sec. 11.131, and an unmarried surviving spouse may keep it on stated conditions. A homestead donated by a charity falls under Sec. 11.132, where the exempt share follows the rating. Sec. 11.133 fully exempts the home of the surviving spouse of a service member killed in the line of duty.

How the layers combine

Picture a stack that grows with your circumstances. Each layer applies only to the units that grant it.

  • Any residence homestead owner: the mandatory $140,000 school district exemption.
  • Owner aged 65 or older, or disabled: the same $140,000 plus $60,000, along with the school tax freeze.
  • Disabled veteran: a separate exemption on one property, from $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, or total at a 100 percent rating on the residence homestead.
  • Any owner in a unit with a local option: a percentage exemption of up to 20 percent of value on top.

These are separate provisions. If you fit two groups, ask the appraisal district how they work together on your actual bill.

What to bring to the appraisal district

Bring proof you own the house and proof it is your main home, such as a utility bill. Each district decides what it accepts, so call before you go. File before the spring cutoff so the exemption reaches the bill mailed that fall.

  • The deed, or for an heir the ownership affidavit and death certificate.
  • A current utility bill showing the property address.
  • For age, disability or a VA rating, whatever proof the district accepts. Ask which documents it wants before you file.
  • The form that matches your exemption: 50-114 for homestead, 50-135 for the disabled veteran exemption.

A disabled veteran exemption does not always have to wait for the next spring cycle, because Sec. 11.22 allows late applications for up to five years after the delinquency date.

When and where to apply

Applications go to the county appraisal district, not the school district or the state. For the general homestead exemption, filing must come before May 1, and April 30 is also the cutoff for some other exemption and special-appraisal applications.

  • Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114.
  • The disabled veteran exemption under Sec. 11.22 uses Form 50-135.
  • Under Sec. 11.22 an applicant has up to five years past the delinquency date, and the surviving spouse of a veteran with a donated homestead gets two.

Value notices for single-family homesteads start around April 1. Disputing the number is a separate step from claiming the exemption and has its own cutoff, usually May 15 unless 30 days after delivery falls later.

Homestead exemption when you sell

The exemption leaves with your ownership, but that year's tax lien stays on the land. It attaches January 1 for taxes, penalties and interest, so unpaid amounts are normally cleared at closing.

Whoever owned the property on January 1 is liable for the year's bill and can be sued after selling. Delinquency starts February 1 for bills mailed in October, with penalty and interest added.

If the sale involves back taxes, unrecorded heirs or a house you have moved out of, get a payoff from the tax office and confirm your exemption status with the district before you list. A cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender, but the tax payoff still gets settled at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Texas homestead exemption automatic?

No. You apply with Form 50-114 at the appraisal district, in general before May 1.

Can I get both the $140,000 and the $60,000 school exemptions?

Yes, if you are 65 or older or disabled. The two stack: $140,000 under Sec. 11.13(b) plus $60,000 under Sec. 11.13(c).

Does the 10 percent cap lower my tax rate?

No. It slows growth in appraised value only. Each unit sets its own rate, and new improvements are added on top of the capped value.

Can a surviving spouse keep the over-65 exemption?

In some cases, if the spouse is 55 or older, and the school tax ceiling may continue as well. The appraisal district can confirm your situation.

What if I inherited a house and am not on the deed?

Bring four items to the district: an ownership affidavit, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation.

Texas Property Tax Protest: Deadlines, ARB Hearing and Appeals

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Property Tax Protest sale
  • Turn the Texas Property Tax Protest offer down and you owe us nothing

Property Tax Burden Too High? Get a Cash Offer for Your Texas House

If taxes are part of why you want out, a cash sale pays them at closing. Tell us about the house.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

To protest your Texas appraisal, file written notice with the appraisal review board by May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered to you, whichever is later. That rule is in Tax Code Sec. 41.44(a)(1). This guide follows the Comptroller's protest page and Tax Code Chapters 41 and 42 through the ARB hearing and appeals.

Tired of the tax bills?
We buy as-is, pay taxes from the proceeds and charge no commission.

Protest deadline

For most owners the cutoff is May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever comes later. The 30 days run from the date the district mails the notice, not the day it reaches you.

The district must send a notice of appraised value by May 1 (April 1 for a residence homestead), or soon after, whenever the value is higher than last year. The notice explains how to file and mentions the informal conference option. Open it the day it arrives and write down the mailing date.

How to file a protest

File Form 50-132, Property Owner's Notice of Protest, with the appraisal review board (ARB). The form is optional, though. A written notice that names the property, the owner and some disagreement with a district decision is enough.

  • Use Form 50-162 if you want an agent to represent you at the hearing.
  • Lessees who must reimburse the owner's taxes may protest if the owner does not.
  • Off-shore workers and full-time military members may be entitled to file late.

Keep a copy and proof of the filing date, since the deadline controls whether you get a hearing.

What you can protest

The appraised value is the usual subject, but you can contest any district action touching your property. Hearing topics include value, exemptions, special appraisal qualification and the circuit breaker limitation.

Many owners ask whether the tax bill itself can be protested. It cannot. Neither the ARB nor the appraisal district sets your taxes, and the ARB cannot consider your personal finances. Its job is to certify value as the market dictates.

Where the protest fits in the tax year

Protest season sits between the spring notices and the summer roll. The ARB starts hearing protests around May 15 and approves the appraisal records by July 20. By July 25 the chief appraiser certifies the roll to each taxing unit. If more than 5 percent of total appraised value is still under protest, the ARB may hold off on approval.

Units then adopt rates by about the end of September, and bills go out October 1. A successful protest lowers the value those rates are applied to. It leaves the rate alone.

  • Spring: value notice arrives and the protest window opens.
  • Late spring and summer: informal conferences and ARB hearings.
  • July: records approved and roll certified.
  • October: bills mailed, with the tax due by the following January 31.

Between filing and the hearing

You can ask the appraisal district for an informal conference, and many protests end right there. If yours does not, it moves on to a formal hearing.

The ARB must give at least 15 days' notice of the hearing date, time, place and subject. At least 14 days before, the district must send the Taxpayer Assistance Pamphlet, the ARB procedures it adopted and a statement that you may request copies of the evidence it plans to use. You may appear in person, by phone or videoconference, or file a written affidavit. In counties above 120,000 people, give an email address or number and you will get electronic notices and reminders.

Evidence that helps at a hearing

Bring proof of value. Saying the district is wrong will not carry the day.

  • Photographs of your property and comparable ones.
  • Repair receipts or estimates.
  • Sales price records, such as listings or closing statements.
  • Median level of appraisal calculations, for an equal and uniform protest.
  • Affidavits, engineering reports, surveys and deed records.

You decide whether to present before or after the district's representative. Each side may present evidence, question witnesses and offer an opinion of value. Stick to facts about value. The ruling covers only the tax year at issue.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If you miss the deadline

A late protest can still get a hearing if you show good cause before the ARB approves the appraisal records. After approval, or without good cause, the right to protest can end.

A few narrower late routes exist, and each requires that the tax not be delinquent.

  • You never received a notice the district was required to send.
  • A motion for correction when a residence homestead was valued at least one-fourth too high.
  • A motion for correction when other property was valued at least one-third too high.
  • A clerical error, duplicate appraisal or ownership error, which can reach back through the current year and five earlier years.
  • A joint motion with the chief appraiser, which the ARB approves if both agree.

Limited binding arbitration

This narrow tool targets process problems. After you file a protest, if you believe the ARB or the chief appraiser skipped a procedural requirement, you can ask the Comptroller's office for limited binding arbitration to compel compliance. It does not reopen the value itself.

If you simply disagree with the value, stay with the hearing and the appeal routes in the table below.

Who can speak for you

An owner or lessee may name a representative on Form 50-162, Appointment of Agent for Property Tax Matters. An agent can attend, present evidence and question the district's witness for you.

The hearing is not the place to argue about the size of your bill or your income. The ARB may weigh general economic and environmental influences on value but not an owner's personal finances. The Comptroller's office cannot advise on a matter under protest, so direct questions about a live case to the appraisal district or the ARB.

After the hearing the ARB sends a written order by email or certified mail. Keep it, because every appeal deadline runs from the day you receive it.

Appealing the ARB's decision

Three routes are open, and the written order comes by email or certified mail.

Appeal options after an ARB order
OptionDeadline from the orderNotes
State district courtPetition within 60 days of receiving the orderCounty where the property sits; consult an attorney first
Regular binding arbitrationRequest to the Comptroller within 60 days of noticeHomestead at any value, or property of $5 million or less; deposit required
State Office of Administrative HearingsNotice to chief appraiser within 30 days; $1,500 deposit within 90 daysARB value over $1 million; value or unequal appraisal only; not industrial property

Whichever you choose, pay at least the undisputed tax before the delinquency date. After a hearing, a court may excuse prepayment if you file an oath of inability to pay.

Protesting when you plan to sell

It can pay off. Appraised value drives the tax bill that gets prorated at closing, so a lower value for the year lowers the amount owed. When the ARB rules in your favor, the chief appraiser notifies the taxing units, and the units send any refund if the taxes were already paid.

Tell your closing agent about a pending protest. If the hearing is still ahead when you close, ask how the title company will handle the proration, since the final value may not be known yet. A buyer paying cash may be more flexible on timing than one waiting on a lender, but the protest itself belongs to the owner of record, so keep the paperwork and the filing proof where you can find them.

Special ARB panels hear commercial, utility, industrial and multifamily property above a value threshold. Single-family owners will not reach it.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Texas protest deadline?

May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever is later. The 30 days run from the mailing date.

Do I need a lawyer to protest in Texas?

No. You can file a simple written notice and appear yourself, and Form 50-162 lets you name an agent if you prefer. Talk to an attorney before filing a district court petition.

Can I protest my tax rate?

No. The ARB hears value and related district actions, and it does not set rates. Taxing units adopt rates after notice and hearing.

What if I miss the protest date?

Ask the ARB for a late hearing and show good cause before it approves the appraisal records. Some narrower correction motions also exist, as long as taxes are not delinquent.

How long do I have to appeal an ARB order?

Within 60 days of receiving the order for district court or regular binding arbitration, and within 30 days for the SOAH notice if the ARB value is over $1 million.

Texas Tax Deed Sales: Redemption Rights, Premiums and Excess Proceeds

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Tax Deed Sales sale

Delinquent Taxes on Your Texas House? Get a Cash Offer Before a Sale

A cash sale can pay delinquent taxes before a tax sale. Tell us about the house and any sale date.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

After a Texas tax sale, a former owner of a homestead can redeem the property on or before the second anniversary of the purchaser's deed filing, but must pay a premium of 25 percent in the first year and 50 percent in the second. Other property has only 180 days, and the premium cannot exceed 25 percent. These rules come from Tax Code Chapter 34.

Tax sale coming up?
Tell us the sale date. We buy as-is and can close quickly, with no commission.

How a Texas property goes to a tax sale

Each year's taxes are secured by a lien that arises on the first day of January, and a bill left unpaid can end in a suit and then an auction of the property. The sale is a tax foreclosure auction, and the winning bidder receives a deed afterward.

The ladder runs in order: delinquency notices, an optional installment plan, then a suit by the taxing unit, with court costs added to the bill. Once a bill goes delinquent, the cost climbs. An initial penalty and interest charge is added, the penalty grows each month until July, and interest has no ceiling. Collection attorneys hired by the unit can add a further charge.

Who runs the sale and where it is held

Tax foreclosure sales are auctions, typically run by the constable or an agent the taxing unit hires.

Sale notices appear on the county clerk or county tax office websites. Because each taxing unit and county handles notices its own way, call the tax office that bills the property instead of trusting a general list. The lien survives a change of ownership, so a buyer at an ordinary sale who skips the tax check can end up with the liability.

Can the former owner get the property back?

Yes, in a limited window, and the cost depends on the kind of property. Tax Code Section 34.21 governs redemption.

Redemption rules for land auctioned for taxes
Kind of propertyRedemption periodPremium
Homestead, agricultural or mineral interestTwo years after the buyer's deed is filed25 percent in the first year, 50 percent in the second
Other property180th day after the deed is filedNot over 25 percent

On top of that the owner repays the winning bid, the deed recording fee and the back charges. The purchaser must itemize those costs within 10 days of a written request, so a redeeming owner should put the request on paper.

Excess proceeds

Money left over once the tax debt and costs are paid is called excess proceeds, and the former owner has two years from the sale to claim them. Sections 34.03 and 34.04 of the Tax Code govern the process.

If you suspect money is waiting for you, contact the court that ordered the sale and the tax office. Keep proof of your ownership and your current mailing address with your claim. Heirs of a deceased owner should be ready to show how they inherited, since the claim follows the same ownership questions that arise in probate.

What a buyer should check before bidding

A buyer should confirm what the deed will and will not do, because the redemption right can reopen the deal after the sale.

  • Find out from the tax office which units' taxes the sale covers.
  • Check whether the property is a homestead, farmland or has a mineral interest, since these have the longer redemption period.
  • Review the county records for other liens. The comptroller files state tax liens with the county clerk, who records them in the state tax lien book.
  • Plan for the possibility of an occupant. If someone is living there, expect to need a court case to get possession.

The county clerk is the county recorder, so the clerk's office is also where the deed will be recorded afterward.

How an owner can avoid a tax sale

Pay before the delinquency date or work out a payment plan. Plans on delinquent bills can run as long as 36 months with some collectors, and a homestead owner is entitled to one.

Penalty and interest waivers exist for many cases, but they require quick payment and a written request, so ask the collector for the exact deadlines on your bill. Older or disabled homeowners can split delinquent tax into four installments, and owners with a VA disability rating may qualify for an exemption. If you are behind and thinking of selling, a sale that pays the tax at closing ends the lien problem before a lawsuit begins.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house with a tax sale looming

A buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent taxes are paid. A seller with unpaid tax should get a payoff number from the title company and pay the tax from closing funds.

The January 1 owner owes that year's tax, and a suit can still reach that person after a sale. Get the paid-in-full records from the tax office after closing and keep them.

The property tax calendar

Values are fixed on January 1, bills are mailed near October 1, and a split payment lets an owner pay half in November and the balance in June.

Most owners need to pay by January 31, because taxes unpaid on February 1 are delinquent. Late-mailed bills get a later delinquency date. An owner who disagrees with the appraised value takes that dispute to the appraisal review board, generally by mid-May. After the board, an owner can appeal to district court, binding arbitration, or the state's administrative hearings office when the board value tops $1,000,000.

  • Section 23.23 caps yearly increases in a homestead's appraised value at 10 percent.
  • Section 11.26 can freeze school tax for an older or disabled homeowner.
  • An owner who appeals should still pay the amount not in dispute on time.

Help for owners who are behind

Ask the county tax assessor-collector about installment plans, waivers and exemptions before a suit is filed. Many taxing units contract with the assessor-collector, so one office often handles the bill for several units.

Older and disabled homeowners can pay delinquent amounts in installments, with a 6 percent charge on the late installment and monthly interest. Owners with a VA disability rating should ask the appraisal district about the exemption that matches that rating.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

If you get a notice of tax suit or sale

Act on it the same week. Call the tax office named on the notice, ask for the full payoff with court costs included, and ask whether the collector offers a payment plan for the delinquent years. Collection in Texas moves from notices to a plan to a lawsuit, and each step adds expense, so the cheapest moment to resolve a debt is the earliest one.

  • Write down the cause number and the court named on any suit papers.
  • Ask the clerk of that court how an excess proceeds claim would be filed.
  • Keep copies of every payment receipt, since the owner of record remains answerable for the year's tax.
  • If you plan to sell, give the title company the tax office's payoff letter right away.

Heirs and family members sometimes learn about a delinquent bill only after the owner has died. In that situation the first job is to sort out who holds title, because the person who can negotiate with the tax office is the owner or someone authorized to act for the estate.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a redemption period after a Texas tax sale?

Yes. Homestead, farm and mineral property carries a two-year window. Other property gets roughly half a year.

What premium does a redeeming owner pay?

For the two-year category, the premium is 25 percent if the owner redeems in year one and 50 percent in year two. Other property carries a premium of no more than 25 percent.

Usually on February 1 following the bill year, when penalty and interest start to run.

Texas Real Estate Agent Commission: What the Law Says and Your Options

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Texas Real Estate Agent Commission: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Real Estate Agent Commission sale

Skip the Agent Commission: Get a Cash Offer for Your Texas House

Our cash offers carry no agent commission and no fees. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas law does not set real estate commission rates. The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) says on its consumer page that it does not regulate fees paid to any license holder, and that all fees are set by your agreement with each professional. The TREC resale contract says the same about brokerage compensation.

Want to avoid the commission?
Our cash offers carry zero commission, zero fees and zero closing costs, and we buy as-is.
Get My Cash Offer →

Is there a set commission rate in Texas?

No. The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) does not regulate the fees paid to any license holder, including buyer's agents, seller's agents, brokers, inspectors and appraisers. Every fee comes from your agreement with that professional. Anyone quoting a statewide percentage as a legal rate is describing a habit, not a rule.

Read the fees in any representation or service agreement before you sign it.

Buyer agreement rules in 2026

Under changes from the 89th Texas Legislative Session to the Real Estate License Act, a license holder working with a residential buyer needs a written agreement before showing a home. If no home will be shown, the agreement is needed before the agent presents an offer for the buyer. The changes apply as of January 1, 2026.

The agreement has to state the amount or rate of the broker's compensation and how it will be figured. It also has to say in conspicuous language that broker compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable. Commercial buyers and tenants fall outside the written-agreement rule.

  • Services the license holder will provide.
  • An end date for the agreement.
  • Whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • Whether the license holder represents the buyer.
  • The compensation amount or rate and how it is determined.

How long a showing-only agreement can last

A non-representation, showing-only agreement can run no more than 14 days and must be non-exclusive. A full representation agreement can narrow the services an agent offers, such as limiting them to showings, but cannot waive the minimum duties owed to a client.

For a Texas seller, the effect shows up in the offers you receive. A buyer's agent now arrives with a signed agreement that spells out how that agent expects to be paid, so the question of who covers that fee comes up early in negotiation instead of late.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What agents owe you, and where to complain

Brokers and sales agents must put the client's interests above all others, acting as fiduciaries. The minimum services are telling the client any material information about the property or transaction, answering questions, presenting offers and counteroffers, and treating all parties honestly and fairly.

Agents must hand you the Information About Brokerage Services form the first time you discuss a specific property, along with the Consumer Protection Notice. If you think an agent is not treating you fairly, you can file a complaint with TREC, which can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. TREC's license holder lookup shows whether a person holds an active license and any discipline.

Can an agent rebate part of the commission?

Yes. A license holder may rebate part of the compensation to a party in the transaction without violating the license act or rules. If the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent, the agent must first get the consent of the party the agent does represent, under Rule 535.147(d).

An agent who advertises a rebate must follow Rule 535.155, and a rebate may be limited by the buyer's lender. A listing broker also may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without a broker license. An attorney acting as buyer's agent is one example.

Open houses and showings

These can change who an agent works for. An agent hosting an open house who belongs to the listing broker's office only has to disclose that the agent represents the owner. A showing agent from another brokerage must hand over the Information About Brokerage Services form and sign a written agreement with a visiting buyer before the buyer starts viewing the home.

A buyer who refuses to sign cannot be shown the property, and license holders can face discipline for skipping the written agreement. As a seller, expect a stranger at your open house to be asked to sign paperwork at the door. That is a legal requirement for the agent and not a sign of anything wrong with your listing.

Two references to subagency were removed from the License Act. Subagency has not disappeared as a legal idea, so ask your broker or an attorney if a situation seems to involve it.

Commission sharing and trust accounts

A listing broker may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without holding a broker license. When an attorney represents a buyer, the listing broker must still present the attorney's offer to the seller and tell the seller about the prohibition. The seller and buyer may work out payment to a Texas attorney between themselves.

A listing broker may agree to reduce the commission at a seller's request without breaking the splitting prohibition. Brokers who hold earnest money or other funds in a trust account must provide a monthly accounting when there has been activity, and must keep trust and escrow records for four years from the date the record is received or created.

  • Ask the broker where earnest money will be held.
  • Ask how a commission reduction would be written into the listing agreement.
  • Ask whether any buyer's attorney is involved, and how that attorney is paid.

What to compare before you sign a listing agreement

Put each offer on the same footing by comparing what reaches you after every cost. Commission is one line. Repairs, seller concessions, closing costs and any compensation you agree to pay toward the buyer's agent are others, and each is a contract term you can negotiate.

Where each commission-related term lives
TermWhere it is set
Listing broker feeYour agreement with the broker, not set by TREC
Buyer agent compensationWritten buyer agreement, stated as amount or rate
Rebates to a partyRule 535.147(d) consent rule
Representation and dutiesInformation About Brokerage Services form

Ask your agent which of these appear in the paperwork you are asked to sign, and get each in writing.

Selling without paying an agent commission

You can list with a broker, sell yourself, or sell to a buyer who purchases directly, and each carries different costs and duties. A sale without a listing broker has no listing commission, but it also has no agent handling showings, paperwork or negotiation. TREC's contract forms are written for license holders, and complex or specialized situations may call for an attorney.

If the sale involves a buyer's agent, that agent's written agreement with the buyer states how the agent expects to be paid, and you can ask to see how it applies to your sale before you accept an offer.

A direct cash sale to a buyer who is not using an agent skips the commission line altogether, and often the repair requests and lender timelines too. Compare the net you would receive, not the headline price.

Frequently asked questions

Is real estate commission set by law in Texas?

No. TREC does not regulate fees paid to any license holder, and all fees are set by your agreement with each professional.

Must a Texas buyer sign something with an agent before touring a home?

Yes, for residential buyers. A written agreement is required before showing a home or, if none is shown, before presenting an offer.

Does the written buyer agreement say how the agent gets paid?

Yes. It must state the compensation amount or rate, how it is determined, and conspicuous wording that compensation is not set by law and is negotiable.

Can an agent give back part of a commission?

Yes. A rebate to a party is permitted, and the agent's own client must consent first when the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent.

Where do I complain about an agent?

File a complaint with TREC, which can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. Disputes over who gets earnest money are outside what TREC decides.

Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale: State and Federal Rules

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale sale
  • Turn the Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling Your Texas Home? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and close on your timeline. Tell us about the house.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has no state income tax, and the federal home sale exclusion lets many sellers exclude the first $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly. The Texas Comptroller states that Texas has no state income tax, and IRS Publication 523 sets the exclusion and its tests. This guide summarizes those tests.

Ready to sell?
We buy as-is with no commission, and you choose the closing date.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Texas tax profit from selling a house?

No. Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale adds nothing to a state return because there is no state return to file.

The federal government is the only income tax collector in a Texas home sale. Texas homeowners still deal with property taxes at closing, covered below, but those are charges for owning the house and not a tax on profit.

The federal exclusion for a home sale

The tax-free gain is capped at $250,000 for one filer and $500,000 for spouses filing together. The cap applies to profit only. Profit is what remains after subtracting adjusted basis from the amount realized.

Basis starts with the cost of the house, including sales tax and purchase expenses. Improvements that add value raise it, while items like insurance reimbursements for casualty losses reduce it. A Texas owner who finished a garage apartment or replaced a roof should dig out those receipts. A long-held house with no upgrades tends to carry a low basis and therefore a larger gain.

Losses get no relief. A loss on personal-use property, a home included, is not deductible.

The ownership and use tests

Eligibility turns on ownership and use. Each is measured over the five-year window that ends on the closing date.

Federal home-sale exclusion tests
TestRule
OwnershipTwo years of ownership inside the window
UseTwo years living there as a main residence inside the window
OverlapThe two years of ownership and use can come from different periods
Spouses filing jointlyOne spouse can satisfy ownership; each spouse must satisfy use
Back-to-back salesGenerally blocked if another home's gain was excluded within the prior two years
Extended official dutyWindow can be suspended up to a decade for service members, Foreign Service and intelligence personnel

Publication 523 lists partial-exclusion situations and exceptions.

Estimating your gain before you list

Work through the pieces in order and keep paper copies of each.

  • Start with what you paid for the house, plus purchase-related costs such as sales tax that count as part of basis.
  • Add the cost of improvements that added value, and subtract items that reduce basis, such as insurance reimbursements for casualty losses.
  • Take the amount you expect to realize from the sale and subtract adjusted basis to get the gain.
  • Compare that gain with the $250,000 or $500,000 ceiling if you pass both tests.
  • Only the part above the ceiling, if any, goes into the capital gain rate bands.

Sellers in Texas often forget that a home bought decades ago with little paper trail can still have a documented basis through closing statements and permit records. County clerk deed records and your original settlement statement are a good place to start.

Federal rates on gain above the exclusion

A long-term gain on a Texas house is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income. The 2025 thresholds are below.

  • The 0 percent band ends at $48,350 of taxable income for single and separate filers, $96,700 for joint filers, and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • The 15 percent band runs above those levels to $533,400 single, $300,000 separate, $600,050 joint, and $566,700 head of household.
  • Income past the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent on the excess.

Depreciation claimed while the house was a rental can be taxed at up to 25 percent as unrecaptured section 1250 gain. Short-term results are taxed like wages. Thresholds change by year, so look up the figures that match the year your sale closes.

Inherited or rented houses

The simple exclusion story shifts in both cases. For an inherited house, basis is not simply what the heir paid, and Publication 551 covers it. Property acquired from a decedent also has special holding-period rules, described in Publication 544.

For a house that spent years as a rental, depreciation reduces basis, and Publication 523 handles homes with rental or business use. Title questions for heirs are covered on this site's Texas affidavit of heirship and probate pages.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When you have to report the sale

Report the sale whenever a Form 1099-S arrives, even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and whenever some gain cannot be excluded. Reporting goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

A seller who carried the financing over later years may spread the gain using the installment method, and the home-sale exclusion stays available in that case. Large taxable gains can also trigger estimated payments, and Publication 505 covers that rule.

The one-year holding rule

It is a separate clock from the exclusion tests. An asset kept for more than a year yields a long-term result, and one kept a year or less yields a short-term result taxed at ordinary rates. Counting begins the day after acquisition and includes the sale day.

Picture two sellers. One lived in a house for 18 months and then sold: the holding period is long-term, yet the two-year exclusion tests are unmet. Another owned for 25 months but rented the place out for most of that time: ownership is satisfied while use may not be. Mark both dates on a calendar well ahead of any contract.

Gifts and inherited property get special treatment, and Publication 544 covers them.

Texas charges at closing

Property tax is the main one. Local units, not the state, levy it, and appraisal districts value each parcel annually as of January 1. Because that is the date the year's lien attaches, a buyer's title company will want it settled.

Request the tax certificate early and compare it to what the county tax assessor-collector shows. Unpaid bills carry penalty and interest.

Closing also brings a federal filing detail to know early. If you receive a Form 1099-S, the IRS has a record of the sale whether or not you owe anything. Matching your return to that form avoids notices later, and a tax preparer can check the entries against your settlement statement.

Before closing, collect the original settlement statement from your purchase, receipts for major improvements and any records of casualty claims. Hand copies to your preparer right after the sale, while the paperwork is easy to find. A cash sale closes on a shorter timeline, so gather these papers before you accept an offer rather than after. If the sale produces a gain above the exclusion, ask the preparer whether estimated payments are needed so the first bill is not a surprise. Set aside the likely tax from the proceeds at closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Texas capital gains tax on real estate?

No. Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale produces no state capital gains return. The federal rules still apply.

How long must I live in a Texas home to avoid federal tax on the gain?

At least two years of both ownership and use inside the five years before closing. The months need not be consecutive, and the two periods may be different stretches.

What is the exclusion for a married couple selling a Texas house?

$500,000 of gain on a joint return. One spouse can meet the ownership test, but each spouse must meet the use test on their own.

Can I deduct a loss when I sell my Texas home for less than I paid?

No. Losses from the sale of personal-use property, including your home, are not tax deductible.

Where do I report a Texas home sale?

On Form 8949 and Schedule D when reporting is required, which includes any sale that generated a Form 1099-S. Publication 523 has the worksheets. A tax professional can confirm what fits your facts.

Cash Home Buyers in Texas

Selling a Texas Investment Property? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Under Section 1031, an exchange of real property held for business or investment solely for other business or investment real property of like kind generally defers recognition of gain or loss. Texas has no state income tax, so the issue is federal. This guide uses the IRS real estate tax tips page and Publication 523.

Selling a rental?
We buy rental and investment houses as-is, occupied or vacant, with no commission.
Get My Cash Offer →

Section 1031 exchanges for Texas real estate

It is a federal tax rule that lets an owner of business or investment real property swap it for other business or investment real property and generally skip recognizing the gain or loss at that time. You recognize gain only to the extent you also receive cash or other non-like-kind property, and you cannot recognize a loss. Texas owners use the same federal rule as everyone else.

Since January 1, 2018, the rule covers real property only. Exchanges of equipment, vehicles, artwork, collectibles and patents no longer qualify, apart from certain mutual ditch, reservoir and irrigation stock. A Texas rental house, apartment building, office or tract of land can qualify. Real property held primarily for sale does not.

A tax adviser or a qualified intermediary should confirm how the rule applies to your sale before you list.

Which properties are like-kind

Real properties are generally like-kind to each other, whether improved or unimproved. An apartment building would generally be like-kind to another apartment building, and properties qualify when they share the same nature or character, even if grade or quality differs.

One limit applies to every investor: real property in the United States is not like-kind to real property outside the United States. A Texas duplex can be swapped for land in another state, but not for a property abroad.

  • Qualifies: a Texas rental house exchanged for a fourplex held as an investment.
  • Qualifies: unimproved land exchanged for improved commercial property, if both are held for business or investment.
  • Does not qualify: a house you hold mainly to resell, or a house you use solely as your personal residence.

The 45-day and 180-day deadlines

A deferred exchange has two clocks that start when you transfer the property you give up. Replacement property must be identified within 45 days, and received by the earlier of 180 days or the due date of your tax return, including extensions, for the year of the transfer.

Timing rules for a deferred exchange
StepDeadlineRequirement
Identify replacement propertyWithin 45 days of the transferSigned written document, clear description, sent to the right person
Receive replacement propertyEarlier of day 180 or the return due dateCounts the due date with extensions
Report the exchangeWith the return for the transfer yearFile Form 8824

For real property, the written identification must describe it by legal description, street address or a distinguishable name. If you receive the replacement property before day 45 ends, you are treated as meeting the identification rule. Because the 180-day period can be cut short by the return due date, an exchange that closes late in the year may need an extension of the tax return to use the full 180 days.

Using a qualified intermediary

In a deferred exchange, a qualified intermediary (QI) lets the transfer of the property given up and the receipt of replacement property be treated as a like-kind exchange.

Related parties and your agents cannot serve as the QI. They are called disqualified persons, and Publication 544 has the details. If the QI causes you to miss a timing rule, the transaction does not qualify as a deferred exchange, and the gain may be taxable in the year you transferred the property. A narrow exception exists when a QI defaults because of bankruptcy or receivership.

Pick the intermediary before the sale closes. The Texas side of that process is the same as any sale: a title company, a deed recorded with the county clerk where the property sits, and clear records.

Can you exchange your Texas home?

Not a house you used only as your personal residence. Section 1031 does not apply to real property you gave up if it was used solely as your personal residence at the time of the exchange.

A different rule may help. If you owned and used the property as your main home for at least a total of 2 years during the 5-year period ending on the date of the exchange, Section 121 may let you exclude part or all of the gain. Publication 523 explains how that exclusion works.

A house used partly as a home and partly for business or investment is split, with two separate Form 8824 worksheets: one for the home part and one for the business or investment part. Rental houses in Texas that were once your home, or the reverse, deserve a tax adviser's review before you sign a contract.

Texas steps that still apply

The federal rule changes how gain is taxed, not how a Texas sale is carried out. The deed still has to be signed and acknowledged before a notary, or sworn before two witnesses, and it is recorded with the county clerk of the county where the property lies.

The Texas property tax calendar runs on its own track. A tax lien for each year attaches January 1, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid, so a title company will settle any tax owed from the sale funds. Texas has no state property tax, since local governments set rates and collect the money.

  • Gather the legal description early, because real property must be identified that way or by street address.
  • Ask the county appraisal district and tax office for the tax status of both the old and new property.
  • Keep a copy of the signed identification letter and the date you sent it.

On closing day the title company handles the deed, the payoff of any loan and the transfer of funds to the intermediary. Bring your identification, the legal description and the name of your intermediary so the sale proceeds go to the right place and are never paid to you directly. Ask the title officer to confirm the closing date in writing.

If you are weighing a quick cash sale of an investment house instead, tax treatment differs, so talk to a tax adviser first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to the deferred gain

The gain is deferred, not erased. You file Form 8824 with your return for the year you transferred property in a like-kind exchange, and the form reports the deferred gain or loss.

An exchange with a related party carries a two-year rule. Related parties include a spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, brother or sister, and related entities such as certain corporations, partnerships, trusts and estates. If either side disposes of the property received in such an exchange before the date 2 years after the last transfer, the deferred gain or loss must be reported for the year of the disposition, unless an exception on the form applies. You also file Form 8824 for the two years after a related party exchange.

Frequently asked questions

Does Texas have its own 1031 exchange rules?

The like-kind rule is federal, found in Internal Revenue Code Section 1031. Texas deeds are still recorded with the county clerk, but the like-kind tax treatment comes from federal law.

How long do I have to identify replacement property?

Within 45 days after you transfer the property you give up. The identification must be in writing, signed and clearly described.

How long do I have to close on the replacement property?

By the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the due date of your tax return, including extensions, for the year of the transfer.

Can I do a 1031 exchange on a house I live in?

No, if it was used solely as your personal residence at the time of the exchange. Section 121 may exclude gain if you owned and used it as your main home for 2 of the last 5 years.

Which form reports a like-kind exchange?

Form 8824, filed with your return for the year of the transfer.

Texas housing at a glance

Texas had 31,709,821 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 8.8% from the April 2020 base, and 12,848,245 housing units. Statewide figures show the big picture but say nothing about one street, so treat them as background for a sale and not as a valuation.

Texas added about 2.56 million residents between the April 2020 base of 29,149,498 and July 2025. Housing supply follows people, and builders took out 210,217 building permits in 2025. The state is large, so growth is uneven: a metro suburb and a rural county can sit at opposite ends of the same statewide average.

FHFA house price index for Texas

The FHFA index for Texas stood at 450.76 not seasonally adjusted and 444.25 seasonally adjusted in the second quarter of 2026, with the first quarter of 1991 set to 100. In plain terms, repeat-sale prices in the state are a little over four and a half times the 1991 starting level.

The index follows price changes in repeat transactions on mortgages that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac bought or guaranteed. It does not report the price of any single house, and it can differ from what a given neighborhood saw. Recent quarters are below.

Reading the two index columns

Owner costs, rents and typical values

The statewide owner-occupied housing unit rate is 62.6% for 2020 to 2024, and the median value of owner-occupied units is $283,800 for the same period. These are survey-based figures for the whole state.

  • Median selected monthly owner costs, 2020 to 2024: $2,106 with a mortgage and $678 without one.
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $1,403.
  • Households, 2020 to 2024: 10,992,816, at 2.69 persons per household.
  • Median household income, 2020 to 2024, in 2024 dollars: $78,476.

The gap between $2,106 and $678 shows how much of ownership cost is the mortgage. Property tax is included in owner costs on both lines, which is why the tax calendar matters when you sell.

Why median values differ from sale prices

The $283,800 median is owners' own estimate of value in a multi-year survey. It lags the market and covers every kind of owner-occupied home, from rural ranch houses to suburban new builds.

The FHFA series is built from transactions, but it is a relative index. It tells you how prices moved against 1991, not what a three-bedroom house is worth today. For a number you can negotiate with, a review of local comparable sales or an appraisal does the work that statewide data cannot.

Property tax and your home's value

Property tax is local in Texas, and January 1 is the valuation date. Your bill depends on the value and the owner of record that day.

  • Notices of value for homesteads arrive in spring, so you can compare a news headline about prices with your own notice.
  • A protest to the appraisal review board is the route when your notice looks higher than local sales support.
  • Rates are set in the fall, ahead of bills.

A homestead also carries a 10 percent yearly cap on appraised value, which keeps a rising market from flowing straight into the taxable base. Age 65 and older owners and disabled owners can have additional exemptions attached to the home, so ask the appraisal district what applies to a property before you quote its taxes to a buyer.

How to price a Texas house

Start local. Pull recent sales of similar houses near yours, note how long each took to sell, and compare their size, age and condition with yours. Then check your appraisal notice, because a buyer will see the same number.

Statewide data can tell you whether the market is rising or flat, but your price comes from nearby sales. If the sales history is thin, an appraisal gives you a defensible figure. Sellers who need speed sometimes accept a lower price from a cash buyer in exchange for skipping showings, repairs and a buyer's loan approval.

What to do before taking an offer

Pull your appraisal notice and ask the county tax office for the current-year payoff. Because the year's lien attaches on January 1, taxes belong in the closing math even if the bill has not been mailed.

  1. Request a payoff statement from your mortgage servicer.
  2. Ask the county tax office what is owed for the current year.
  3. Ask the appraisal district which exemptions are attached to the property.
  4. Gather your deed, survey and any recorded liens so the title company can start work.

What happens at closing

At closing, the sale price pays off your mortgage, the unpaid property tax and any recorded liens first. What is left comes to you. The title company prepares the settlement statement, so review it line by line before you sign.

Expect to hand over the deed, keys and any records a buyer asks for, such as warranties or repair receipts. If a payoff figure changes between the offer and the closing date, the title company recalculates it, and your net proceeds move with it. Ask for an updated estimate a few days before the closing date.

Selling with a mortgage or taxes owed

Owing money does not stop a sale. The payoffs come out of the sale price at closing. The problem comes when the price is lower than the total debt, so add up the mortgage payoff, the tax balance and any liens before you set a price floor.

A cash sale skips the buyer's lender, which removes appraisal and loan approval delays. It does not change what you owe, so the same payoff letters are still needed.

When do tax bills arrive?

Bills go out around October 1. Anything unpaid on February 1 is delinquent, and a bill mailed after January 10 can push that date back. If you sell in the fall or winter, the unpaid current-year bill is usually settled at closing out of your proceeds.

No. The figures report history and offer no forecast. Use local comparable sales to price a particular house.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

In Texas, the county clerk serves as the county recorder, and deeds and other instruments are recorded in the county where the property is located. Local Government Code Sec. 191.001 says so, citing Article V, Section 20 of the Texas Constitution. This guide covers what the statutes say about recording.

Title or lien problem?
We buy as-is, including houses with record or lien issues. Tell us what you found.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which office holds the land records?

Start with the county where the property sits. Its clerk is the official recorder, and that same office also keeps the commissioners court minutes and takes probate filings.

If you live in Dallas but own a house elsewhere, the other county's office is the one to work with. There are 254 counties and every one keeps its own index. A few offer searchable images online while others want you at the counter, so phone ahead.

What kinds of papers end up in the deed records?

Mostly ownership transfers plus the paperwork around them. Expect general and special warranty deeds, quitclaims, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds and tax deeds, along with affidavits, loan releases, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney.

  • Deeds that pass ownership from one party to another.
  • Deeds of trust that secure a loan, and the releases that end them.
  • Notices of an upcoming lender auction.
  • State tax lien notices from the Comptroller, which the clerk enters in a state tax lien book.
  • Court papers that carry title after a death.

Title examiners read the whole sequence, so a cluttered record slows a closing.

Signature and acknowledgment requirements

The grantor signs, and the signature is either acknowledged before an authorized officer or sworn before two subscribing witnesses (Property Code section 12.001(b)). Notaries, clerks and county court judges can all take an acknowledgment.

Without that step the clerk may refuse the filing, and a missing buyer mailing address can add a fee. Also line up the names: a dropped middle initial between the new deed and the last recorded one is enough to raise questions at closing. Attorneys and title companies who draft the deed usually catch this first.

What recording costs

Base amounts come from statute and counties add their own charges. Here is the 2023 schedule.

Deed recording charges, 2023
Recording chargeAmount
First page of an instrument$5.00
Every added page or attachment$4.00
Extra indexed names past five$0.25

Records archiveNo more than $10
Technology and infrastructure$2.00
Filing a foreclosure sale notice$2.00 per notice

Some buyers using grant programs may qualify for a waiver, so ask the clerk about it. The office or its website will have the current schedule.

Other costs at closing

Expect recording charges and little else on the clerk's side. For the full closing cost list, ask your title company.

Property tax is separate. The lien for each year attaches on January 1, and whoever owned the house that day stays liable even after selling. At closing the year's bill is split between buyer and seller, and the title search looks back for any unpaid years.

Liens and sale deeds in the index

Your mortgage is indexed as a deed of trust, and payoff should be followed by a recorded release. A lender that skipped the release leaves a ghost lien that surfaces in a search and may have to be cleared first.

Taxes leave their own marks. The yearly property tax lien needs no filing at all, but a state tax lien is a recorded notice. A tax sale deed is filed too, and its filing date starts the redemption clock: two years for homestead, agricultural and mineral land, at a 25 percent premium in year one and 50 percent in year two, plus costs. Everything else gets 180 days.

  • Mortgage deeds of trust, plus the releases that cancel them.
  • State tax lien notices.
  • Tax foreclosure and sheriff's deeds.
  • Any judgment or contractor claim that the clerk has indexed.

Records after a death or a foreclosure

The paper left by an inherited house varies with the route the family chose. Administration produces an executor's or administrator's deed, a muniment produces the order and the will, and a transfer on death deed produces an affidavit of death and a death certificate. Nobody at the clerk's office can append heirs to the old deed.

Foreclosure has a separate paper trail. A notice goes up at the courthouse and a copy goes to the clerk three weeks or more ahead. Auctions are usually held on the first Tuesday of the month, and the winning buyer's trustee deed is recorded like any other.

What a former owner can reclaim after a sale

Sometimes a sale brings in more than was owed. A former owner has two years after a tax foreclosure to claim the surplus. After a lender's sale, junior lienholders collect first and any remainder goes to the former owner.

A lender whose sale comes up short may sue for the gap within two years, though the borrower can ask for credit at fair market value. Redemption after a lender's sale applies only to certain kinds, such as owners' association assessment liens. Each of these clocks runs from the sale date in the recorded deed.

An occupant who stays after a sale may face an eviction case. That is a court matter, and the buyer's recorded deed is the proof used there.

Asking the clerk for copies

Bring the owner's name exactly as written on the last deed, the property address, and the recording date or instrument number if you have one. Offices search by name or by instrument number, and a title company can order the same copies on your behalf.

Request the vesting deed, each open deed of trust and any release. Plain copies work for your own reading, though a title company may insist on certified ones. Copies are billed per page, so ask what payment the counter accepts.

Why the record matters to a seller

Buyers and their lenders judge a house by what the index shows, not by what the family remembers. A deed that was signed but never filed, a loan paid off years ago with no release on record, or a probate order sitting in the wrong county can each stall a contract for weeks while someone tracks down a fix.

The fixes are ordinary paperwork: a new acknowledgment, a release letter from the old lender, or a certified copy sent to the right office. Most are cheaper and faster when you start before the house is under contract. Even a cash purchase handled through a title company still needs the chain to read cleanly, but there is no lender checklist layered on top, so a clean record usually means a quick closing.

What to do if the records show a problem

Do not guess at the fix. Call the county clerk to learn what is actually on file, then talk to a title company or a Texas real estate attorney about the right corrective instrument. If the issue involves an old lien, contact the lender or the state office that filed the notice and ask for a written release you can record. Give yourself time before listing, since recording and re-indexing at a busy office are not instant.

Checklist before you list

Order a search early. A defect found before listing can be fixed on your schedule, not the buyer's.

  • Make sure the listing name matches the name on the deed.
  • Find the deed of trust and confirm it was paid off or released.
  • Ask about any state tax lien notice.
  • Check the appraisal district record for the owner of record and exemptions.
  • With an inherited house, confirm the probate paper was recorded in the correct county.

None of this costs much, and it can save weeks later.

Frequently asked questions

Who maintains Texas land records?

The county clerk where the land sits. That office records deeds, loan documents, liens and sale notices.

What does it cost to file a deed?

The 2023 schedule runs $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for every added page, plus capped add-ons. Ask the clerk for the current total.

What must a Texas deed carry to be recorded?

The grantor's signature, acknowledged by a notary or another authorized officer, or sworn before two witnesses.

Can a clerk write heirs onto an old deed?

No. A fresh instrument has to be recorded instead, such as an executor's deed, a muniment order or an affidavit of death.

Where do foreclosure notices go?

It must be posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the sale. The clerk charges $2.00 to file it.
